items.title: Variables and basic types
items.concept: A variable is a name pointing to a value. Python infers the type from the value you assign.
items.why: Every later skill—DataFrames, loops, functions, API calls—starts with storing values under names.
items.task: Create four variables: table_name as "sales", batch_size as 5000, is_full_load as False, and threshold as 0.95.
items.starter: # Write the four assignments below
items.solution:
table_name = "sales"
batch_size = 5000
is_full_load = False
threshold = 0.95
hints: Strings need quotes. Booleans are True/False with capital first letter.
items.pitfall: Do not write `table_name == "sales"`; `==` compares values, while `=` assigns a value.

items.title: while loops and stopping conditions
items.concept: A `while` loop repeats while a condition remains true. Something inside must eventually change that condition.
items.why: Useful for pagination, polling, and retry-like control flow, but easy to turn into an infinite loop.
items.task: Starting with page = 1, print pages 1 to 3 using a while loop.
items.starter:
page = 1

# Write a while loop
items.solution:
page = 1

while page <= 3:
    print(page)
    page += 1
hints: The condition is checked before each iteration.
items.pitfall: If `page` never changes, the loop never ends.

items.title: Default and keyword arguments

items.title: Big-O intuition: list vs set membership
items.concept: Big-O describes how work grows with input size. List membership is generally O(n); set membership is average O(1).
items.why: You do not need algorithm competitions, but you should recognize when repeated linear scans make validation unnecessarily slow.
items.task: Rewrite the membership structure so checking many IDs is efficient. Keep the final boolean expression.
items.starter:
allowed_ids = [101, 102, 103, 104]
customer_id = 103

# Improve the membership structure
is_allowed = customer_id in allowed_ids
hints: Use a set when order and duplicates do not matter.
items.pitfall: Do not blindly convert everything to a set; lists preserve order and allow duplicates.

items.title: Linear search
items.concept: Linear search checks items one by one until it finds a match or reaches the end. Its work grows linearly with the number of items: O(n).
items.why: You should recognize the simplest search algorithm before learning when a set/dictionary or sorted search is better.
items.task: Loop through table_names. Set found = True when the target table appears, then stop the loop with break.
items.starter:
table_names = ["customers", "orders", "products"]
target = "orders"
found = False

# Search with a loop
items.solution:
table_names = ["customers", "orders", "products"]
target = "orders"
found = False

for table in table_names:
    if table == target:
        found = True
        break
hints: Use `break` once the target is found.
items.pitfall: For repeated membership checks against a large fixed collection, a set is usually a better lookup structure than rescanning a list every time.

items.title: Deduplicate while preserving order
items.concept: Use a set for fast “have I seen this?” checks and a list for ordered output.
items.why: This combines two data structures for different jobs: hash lookup for membership and a list for stable sequence.
items.task: Create unique_ids from ids, preserving first-seen order.
items.starter:
ids = [3, 1, 3, 2, 1]
seen = set()
unique_ids = []

# Dedupe in order
items.solution:
ids = [3, 1, 3, 2, 1]
seen = set()
unique_ids = []

for item in ids:
    if item not in seen:
        seen.add(item)
        unique_ids.append(item)
hints: Add new items to both structures.
items.pitfall: `list(set(ids))` removes duplicates but does not communicate a first-seen-order guarantee as clearly as the explicit pattern.

items.title: Chunk work into batches
items.concept: Batching partitions a sequence into fixed-size chunks so work can be processed incrementally.
items.why: APIs, database inserts, file operations, and control-plane jobs often need batch limits even when the data engine itself is distributed.
items.task: Loop over ids in chunks of batch_size using slicing and print each batch.
items.starter:
ids = list(range(1, 11))
batch_size = 3

# Process chunks
items.solution:
ids = list(range(1, 11))
batch_size = 3

for start in range(0, len(ids), batch_size):
    batch = ids[start:start + batch_size]
    print(batch)
hints: `range(start, stop, step)` can advance by batch_size.
Slice from start to start + batch_size.
items.pitfall: Do not manually batch row-level Spark processing on the driver; distributed data engines already partition work and should use their native APIs.

    {"order_id": 11, "customer_id": 1},
]

items.title: Binary search intuition
items.concept: Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted search space, giving O(log n) search time.
items.why: You do not need to hand-code it daily, but it is a classic interview concept and builds intuition for indexes and sorted structures.
items.task: Use Python bisect to find the insertion position of target in an already sorted list.
items.starter:
from bisect import bisect_left
values = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
target = 30

# Find insertion/search position
items.solution:
from bisect import bisect_left
values = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
target = 30

position = bisect_left(values, target)
found = position < len(values) and values[position] == target
hints: `bisect_left` returns where the value should be inserted.
items.pitfall: If you must sort an unsorted list just to perform one search, the sort cost can outweigh the binary-search benefit.

items.title: Sorting + stable keys
items.concept: Comparison-based sorting is generally O(n log n). Merge sort and quicksort are the classic mental models; in Python you normally use the built-in stable `sorted` / `.sort()` implementation with an explicit key.
items.why: Sorting appears before deduplication, window logic, merge operations, ordered exports, and many distributed shuffles. A data engineer should know the cost and the stable-sort idea even when the engine performs the sort.
items.task: Sort events first by event_time and then by event_id. Keep the original list unchanged.
items.starter:
events = [
    {"event_id": 3, "event_time": "2026-09-03T10:02:00"},
    {"event_id": 1, "event_time": "2026-09-03T10:01:00"},
    {"event_id": 2, "event_time": "2026-09-03T10:01:00"},

items.title: Two pointers: merge sorted streams
items.concept: The two-pointer pattern advances through two ordered sequences once, giving O(n + m) work instead of repeatedly scanning or re-sorting.
items.why: This is the core idea behind the merge phase of merge sort and ordered merge operations. It is useful interview intuition for sorted files, partitions, timestamps, and incremental streams.
items.task: Merge the two already-sorted ID lists into one sorted list without calling `sorted()` on the combined result.
items.starter:
left = [1, 4, 8, 12]
right = [2, 3, 9, 15]
i = 0
j = 0
merged = []

# Merge with two pointers
items.solution:
left = [1, 4, 8, 12]
right = [2, 3, 9, 15]
i = 0
j = 0
merged = []

while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
    if left[i] <= right[j]:
        merged.append(left[i])
        i += 1
    else:
        merged.append(right[j])
        j += 1

merged.extend(left[i:])
merged.extend(right[j:])
hints: Compare the current item from each list.
When one list is exhausted, append the remaining tail of the other.
items.pitfall: Two pointers only gives this simple linear merge because both inputs are already ordered.

items.title: Sliding window
items.concept: A sliding window updates a metric as the window moves instead of recomputing the whole window from scratch. Many fixed-window problems become O(n).
items.why: Rolling row counts, recent-event thresholds, monitoring windows, and time-series features all use this mental model. SQL and Spark window functions automate much of it, but the underlying algorithm is worth knowing.
items.task: Find the maximum total rows processed across any 3 consecutive batches using a rolling sum.
items.starter:
batch_rows = [120, 80, 200, 150, 90, 210]
window_size = 3

# Compute max_window_total with a sliding sum
items.solution:
batch_rows = [120, 80, 200, 150, 90, 210]
window_size = 3

window_total = sum(batch_rows[:window_size])
max_window_total = window_total

for right in range(window_size, len(batch_rows)):
    window_total += batch_rows[right]
    window_total -= batch_rows[right - window_size]
    max_window_total = max(max_window_total, window_total)
hints: Start with the sum of the first window.
For each move, add the new right value and subtract the value leaving on the left.
items.pitfall: Calling `sum()` on every slice works for small inputs but repeats work and hides the sliding-window idea.

items.title: Prefix sums for fast range totals
items.concept: A prefix-sum array stores cumulative totals. After O(n) preprocessing, any contiguous range sum can be answered in O(1).
items.why: Prefix-style cumulative state appears in running totals, partition statistics, cumulative metrics, and some incremental-processing problems.
items.task: Build prefix so prefix[i] is the total of values before index i. Then compute the sum from start=1 through end=3 inclusive.
items.starter:
rows = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
start = 1
end = 3
prefix = [0]

# Build prefix and compute range_total
items.solution:
rows = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
start = 1
end = 3
prefix = [0]

for value in rows:
    prefix.append(prefix[-1] + value)

range_total = prefix[end + 1] - prefix[start]
hints: Start prefix with 0 so indexes stay convenient.
Range start..end is cumulative-through-end minus cumulative-before-start.
items.pitfall: Be explicit about whether range endpoints are inclusive; off-by-one errors are the main failure mode.

items.title: Heap / priority queue: Top K
items.concept: A heap keeps the smallest or largest priority element accessible efficiently. A size-k heap can track Top K values without fully sorting every item.
items.why: Top customers, largest files, most expensive jobs, newest events, and priority scheduling are common data-engineering patterns. Distributed engines also implement Top K with related ideas.
items.task: Use `heapq.nlargest` to return the 3 files with the largest size_mb values.
items.starter:
import heapq

files = [
    {"name": "a.parquet", "size_mb": 120},
    {"name": "b.parquet", "size_mb": 900},
    {"name": "c.parquet", "size_mb": 450},
    {"name": "d.parquet", "size_mb": 700},
]

# Create top_3
items.solution:

files = [
    {"name": "a.parquet", "size_mb": 120},

items.title: BFS graph traversal
items.concept: Breadth-first search (BFS) explores a graph level by level using a queue. Depth-first search (DFS) explores one branch deeply using recursion or a stack. Both are O(V + E) for a graph represented by adjacency lists.
items.why: Pipeline dependencies, lineage, downstream-impact analysis, and service dependency graphs are graph problems. You should be able to recognize BFS/DFS even if a framework performs the traversal.
items.task: Starting from ingest, use BFS to collect every reachable downstream task exactly once.
items.starter:
from collections import deque

graph = {
    "ingest": ["clean", "audit"],
    "clean": ["model"],
    "audit": [],
    "model": ["publish"],
    "publish": [],
}

# Traverse from ingest
items.solution:
from collections import deque

graph = {
    "ingest": ["clean", "audit"],
    "clean": ["model"],
    "audit": [],
    "model": ["publish"],
    "publish": [],
}

queue = deque(["ingest"])
visited = set()
order = []

while queue:
    node = queue.popleft()
    if node in visited:
        continue
    visited.add(node)
    order.append(node)
    queue.extend(graph.get(node, []))
hints: BFS uses a FIFO queue such as `deque`.
Track visited nodes so shared dependencies or cycles do not make you process a node repeatedly.
items.pitfall: A graph is not necessarily a tree: multiple parents and cycles are possible, so a visited set matters.

items.title: Topological sort for pipeline dependencies
items.concept: Topological sorting produces a valid execution order for a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Kahn's algorithm repeatedly processes nodes whose in-degree is zero.
items.why: Airflow DAGs, dbt models, build systems, orchestration plans, and dependency-aware deployment all rely on this exact graph concept.
items.task: Build a valid task order from the dependency pairs. Use in-degree counts and a queue. Set has_cycle when not every task can be ordered.
items.starter:
from collections import defaultdict, deque

tasks = {"extract", "clean", "model", "publish"}
edges = [
    ("extract", "clean"),
    ("clean", "model"),
    ("model", "publish"),
]

# Kahn topological sort
hints: In-degree means number of incoming dependencies.
Only tasks with in-degree 0 are ready to run.
If nodes remain after the queue empties, there is a cycle.
items.pitfall: A topological order exists only for a DAG. Cyclic dependencies must be rejected or redesigned.

items.title: CASE expression
items.concept: CASE is SQL branching: it returns a value based on ordered conditions.
items.why: Used for bucketing, flags, normalization, and conditional transformations.
items.task: Create size_band: high if amount >= 1000, medium if >= 100, otherwise low.
items.starter:
SELECT
    amount,
    -- add CASE
FROM dbo.sales;
items.solution:
SELECT
    amount,
    CASE
        WHEN amount >= 1000 THEN 'high'
        WHEN amount >= 100 THEN 'medium'
        ELSE 'low'
    END AS size_band
FROM dbo.sales;
hints: Order conditions from most specific/highest threshold downward.
items.pitfall: The first matching WHEN wins.

items.title: ROW_NUMBER for latest row per key
items.concept: Window functions compute values across related rows without collapsing them like GROUP BY.
items.why: Latest-row deduplication is one of the most common DE interview SQL patterns.
items.task: Rank each customer’s rows newest first by updated_at.
items.starter:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    updated_at,
    -- add row number
FROM dbo.customer_updates;
items.solution:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    updated_at,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY customer_id
        ORDER BY updated_at DESC
    ) AS rn
FROM dbo.customer_updates;
hints: PARTITION BY restarts numbering for each customer.
items.pitfall: If timestamps can tie, add a deterministic tie-breaker to ORDER BY.

items.concept: Rank rows inside each business key, then keep rn = 1.

        *,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY customer_id
            ORDER BY updated_at DESC

    FROM dbo.customer_updates
)
SELECT *
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

original.task: Return only the latest record per customer_id from dbo.customer_updates.
original.starter: -- Use a CTE and ROW_NUMBER
original.solution:

        *,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY customer_id
            ORDER BY updated_at DESC

    FROM dbo.customer_updates

FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

items.title: SCD Type 2 mental model
items.concept: SCD Type 2 preserves history by expiring the old dimension row and inserting a new version when tracked attributes change.
items.why: This is a classic data engineering interview topic and a key dimensional-modeling concept.
items.task: Write the UPDATE that expires the current customer row when its city changed. Assume #stage contains customer_id and city, and dim_customer has is_current and valid_to.
items.starter: -- Expire only changed current rows
items.solution:
UPDATE d
SET
    d.is_current = 0,
    d.valid_to = SYSUTCDATETIME()
FROM dbo.dim_customer AS d
INNER JOIN #stage AS s
    ON d.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHERE d.is_current = 1
  AND ISNULL(d.city, '') <> ISNULL(s.city, '');

-- Next step: INSERT a new current version for new/changed business keys.
items.pitfall: SCD2 normally needs both steps: expire old version and insert new version. Use a surrogate dimension key if downstream facts must reference a specific historical version.

items.title: Window deduplication
items.concept: A Spark Window defines partitioning and ordering for window functions such as row_number.
items.why: Latest-record dedupe is a canonical PySpark interview pattern.
items.task: Keep the newest customer update per customer_id using updated_at.
items.starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

# Define window, rank, filter
items.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

w = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(F.col("updated_at").desc())

latest = (
    updates
    .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w))
    .filter(F.col("rn") == 1)
    .drop("rn")
)
items.pitfall: Add a tie-breaker if updated_at is not unique within a business key.

items.title: Idempotent task design
items.concept: An idempotent task can be retried without creating an incorrect duplicate side effect.

items.task: Choose the safer write pattern by replacing the blind append comment with a deterministic overwrite for one partition (pseudocode is fine).
items.starter:
def load_partition(run_date):
    # BAD: append_same_partition_again()
    # Write a retry-safe intent below
    pass
hints: Make the target deterministic from run_date.
Retry should replace/reconcile the same target, not create a second copy.
items.pitfall: Idempotency is a system-design property; syntax alone cannot guarantee it.

items.title: Minimal Python Dockerfile
items.concept: A Dockerfile defines the filesystem and default command for an image layer by layer.
items.why: You should recognize FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, and CMD without needing to memorize advanced container internals.
items.task: Complete a minimal image that copies requirements.txt, installs dependencies, copies job.py, and runs it.
items.starter:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app

# copy requirements and install
# copy job.py
# run job.py
items.solution:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY job.py .

CMD ["python", "job.py"]
hints: Install requirements before copying frequently changing app code to improve layer caching.

items.title: Install/configuration checklist
items.concept: A reliable gateway deployment separates machine readiness, installation, registration, data-source configuration, and operations.
items.why: This is what you need in an interview: explain the sequence and where failures can happen.
items.task: Write the 6 major steps you would follow to deploy a standard gateway on a Windows VM.
items.solution:
1. Prepare a supported, always-on Windows VM close to the data source and verify outbound connectivity.
2. Install any required database drivers/providers on the VM.
3. Install the latest standard on-premises data gateway as a machine administrator.
4. Sign in with the organization work/school account and register a new gateway or join a gateway cluster.
5. In the Power BI/Fabric service, configure the gateway connection/data source and credentials, then map the semantic model/dataflow.
6. Test refresh/query, inspect logs and service health, keep the gateway updated, and use a cluster when high availability is required.
hints: Think machine → drivers → install → register → map → operate.
Standard mode is the general shared/enterprise mode.
items.pitfall: Do not install a production gateway on a laptop that sleeps or disconnects. Treat the gateway VM as infrastructure.

items.title: dbt: parse raw HTTP logs
items.concept: A staging model turns unstable raw text into typed analytical columns.
items.why: Parsing and typing belong close to the source so downstream models can operate on stable contracts.
items.context: Input column: content. Extract ip_address, log_timestamp, url, status_code using DuckDB regex functions.
items.task: Complete stg_access_logs.sql so the raw text becomes four typed columns.
items.starter:
with source as (
  select * from {{ source('raw_data', 'access_logs') }}
),
parsed as (
  select
    regexp_extract(content, '^(\S+)', 1) as ip_address,
    # timestamp,
    # url,
    # status code
  from source
)
select * from parsed
items.solution:
with source as (
  select * from {{ source('raw_data', 'access_logs') }}
),
parsed as (
  select
    regexp_extract(content, '^(\S+)', 1) as ip_address,
    strptime(regexp_extract(content, '\[(.*?)\]', 1), '%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z') as log_timestamp,
    regexp_extract(content, '"GET (.*?) HTTP', 1) as url,
    cast(regexp_extract(content, 'HTTP/1.1" (\d{3})', 1) as int) as status_code
  from source
)
select * from parsed
items.pitfall: Regex extraction can silently return empty strings; test malformed lines explicitly.

items.title: dbt: derive action + product_id
items.concept: Staging models normalize transport-level fields into business-level attributes.
items.why: Business models should not repeatedly parse URLs.
items.context: URLs include /product/105, /add_to_cart/105, /checkout and browse paths.
items.task: Derive action and product_id. Keep product_id NULL when the URL has no product identifier.
items.starter:
select
  *,
  case
    when url like '/product/%' then #
    when url like '/add_to_cart/%' then #
    when url like '/checkout%' then #
    else #
  end as action,
  # product_id
from {{ ref('stg_access_logs_base') }}
items.solution:
select
  *,
  case
    when url like '/product/%' then 'view_product'
    when url like '/add_to_cart/%' then 'add_to_cart'
    when url like '/checkout%' then 'checkout'
    else 'browse'

items.title: pandas: parse the same access logs
items.concept: The same staging contract can be implemented locally with vectorized pandas string extraction.
items.why: Rebuilding one business transformation in several tools makes the underlying data logic portable.
items.context: lines = pd.Series([...]) containing Apache-style GET requests. Produce ip_address, log_timestamp, url, status_code.
items.task: Create a DataFrame with the same staging columns as the dbt model without row-by-row Python loops.
items.starter:
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.DataFrame({"content": lines})
parsed = pd.DataFrame()
parsed["ip_address"] = #
parsed["log_timestamp"] = #
parsed["url"] = #
parsed["status_code"] = #
items.solution:
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.DataFrame({"content": lines})
parsed = pd.DataFrame()
parsed["ip_address"] = raw["content"].str.extract(r'^(\S+)', expand=False)
parsed["log_timestamp"] = pd.to_datetime(raw["content"].str.extract(r'\[(.*?)\]', expand=False), format='%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z', errors='coerce')
parsed["url"] = raw["content"].str.extract(r'"GET (.*?) HTTP', expand=False)
parsed["status_code"] = pd.to_numeric(raw["content"].str.extract(r'HTTP/1.1" (\d{3})', expand=False), errors='coerce').astype('Int64')
hints: Use coercing parsers so malformed rows become observable nulls.
items.pitfall: Avoid apply(lambda row: regex...) when vectorized string operations express the same transformation.

  A[access.log] --> P[pandas parse]
  J[products.json] --> M[merge]
  P --> M
  M --> Q[quality checks]
  Q --> G[daily_revenue.parquet]

items.title: pandas: daily revenue mart
items.concept: merge + filter + groupby reproduces the analytical mart locally.
items.why: You should recognize the same grain and join-cardinality risks outside SQL.
items.context: events has log_timestamp, action, product_id. products has unique product_id and product_price.
items.task: Build daily_revenue with potential_revenue and items_added.
items.starter:
cart = events[#].copy()
enriched = cart.merge(products, #)
daily_revenue = (
  enriched.assign(report_date=#)
    .groupby(#, as_index=False)
    .agg(#)
)
items.solution:
cart = events[events["action"].eq("add_to_cart")].copy()
enriched = cart.merge(products, on="product_id", how="inner", validate="many_to_one")
daily_revenue = (
  enriched.assign(report_date=enriched["log_timestamp"].dt.floor("D"))
    .groupby("report_date", as_index=False)
    .agg(potential_revenue=("product_price", "sum"), items_added=("product_id", "size"))
)
hints: validate=many_to_one protects the dimensional join contract.
items.pitfall: Do not average or sum duplicated product prices caused by a non-unique dimension key.

items.title: PySpark: Bronze → Silver event parsing
items.concept: Bronze preserves raw evidence; Silver parses and types fields using distributed column expressions.
items.why: This is the common lakehouse separation between recoverable raw data and trusted structured data.
items.context: bronze has one string column content with the same access-log format.
items.task: Create silver with ip_address, log_timestamp, url and status_code using pyspark.sql.functions.
items.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

silver = bronze.select(
  F.regexp_extract("content", r"^(\S+)", 1).alias("ip_address"),
  F.to_timestamp(F.regexp_extract("content", r"\[(.*?)\]", 1), "dd/MMM/yyyy:HH:mm:ss Z").alias("log_timestamp"),
  F.regexp_extract("content", r'"GET (.*?) HTTP', 1).alias("url"),
  F.regexp_extract("content", r'HTTP/1.1" (\d{3})', 1).cast("int").alias("status_code"),
)
hints: Do not collect raw log lines to the driver.
items.pitfall: Python UDFs are unnecessary for regex extraction here and usually reduce optimizer visibility.

  B --> S[Silver parsed events]

items.title: PySpark: build the Gold revenue table
items.concept: Gold models apply business logic at a stable reporting grain.
items.why: The same dimensional join and aggregation rules apply whether the engine is DuckDB, pandas or Spark.
items.context: events(action, product_id, log_timestamp); products(product_id, product_price). products is small enough to broadcast.
items.task: Build daily revenue and items_added with a broadcast dimension join.
items.starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

gold = (events
  .filter(#)
  .join(F.broadcast(products), #, #)
  .groupBy(#)
  .agg(#)
)
items.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

gold = (events
  .filter(F.col("action") == "add_to_cart")
  .join(F.broadcast(products), on="product_id", how="inner")
  .withColumn("report_date", F.to_date("log_timestamp"))
  .groupBy("report_date")
  .agg(
    F.sum("product_price").alias("potential_revenue"),
    F.count("*").alias("items_added"),
  )
)
hints: Broadcast only because the product dimension is small.
Group by the declared daily grain.
items.pitfall: Broadcasting a large dimension can exhaust executor memory; it is a physical optimization, not a default rule.

  .join(F.broadcast(products), on="product_id", how="inner")
  .withColumn("report_date", F.to_date("log_timestamp"))
  .groupBy("report_date")
  .agg(
    F.sum("product_price").alias("potential_revenue"),
    F.count("*").alias("items_added"),
  )
)
hints: Broadcast only because the product dimension is small.
Group by the declared daily grain.
original.pitfall: Broadcasting a large dimension can exhaust executor memory; it is a physical optimization, not a default rule.

items.title: PySpark + Delta: idempotent Gold merge
items.concept: MERGE reconciles a recalculated business key into an existing Delta target.
items.why: Idempotent writes are essential for retries, late-arriving data and backfills.
items.context: daily_updates has one row per report_date. Target table: gold.daily_revenue.
items.task: Merge by report_date, updating matches and inserting new dates.
items.starter:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "gold.daily_revenue")
(target.alias("t")
  .merge(daily_updates.alias("s"), #)
  .#
  .#
  .execute())
items.solution:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "gold.daily_revenue")
(target.alias("t")
  .merge(daily_updates.alias("s"), "t.report_date = s.report_date")
  .whenMatchedUpdateAll()
  .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
  .execute())
hints: The daily business key is report_date.
Use matched update + not matched insert.
items.pitfall: Ensure the source is unique on the merge key or a MERGE can be ambiguous or produce unexpected behavior.

items.title: Dockerfile: package a Python app
items.concept: Order Dockerfile layers so dependency installation can be cached independently from frequently changing source code.
items.why: Small, cache-friendly images make CI and deployment faster.
items.context: Files: app.py + requirements.txt. Base image: python:3.12-slim.
items.task: Complete a Dockerfile that installs requirements then runs app.py.
items.starter:
FROM python:3.12-slim

COPY # requirements
WORKDIR /app
RUN # install
COPY # app
CMD # run app
items.solution:
FROM python:3.12-slim

COPY requirements.txt /app/requirements.txt
WORKDIR /app
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY app.py /app/app.py
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
hints: Copy requirements before app.py for better cache reuse.
items.pitfall: Copying the entire repository before pip install invalidates the dependency layer whenever any source file changes.

with mlflow.start_run():

    predicted = model.predict(test_x)
    mlflow.log_param("alpha", alpha)

items.solution:
with mlflow.start_run():
    model.fit(train_x, train_y)
    predicted = model.predict(test_x)
    rmse, mae, r2 = eval_metrics(test_y, predicted)
    mlflow.log_param("alpha", alpha)
    mlflow.log_metric("rmse", rmse)

items.concept: A scheduler triggers training; training logs a candidate model; serving promotes or reloads an approved version.
items.why: Retraining is a pipeline with dependencies, retries and observability—not a while loop in the API server.

with DAG("retrain_model", schedule="@daily", catchup=False) as dag:
    train = PythonOperator(task_id="train", python_callable=train_model)
    evaluate = PythonOperator(task_id="evaluate", python_callable=evaluate_model)
    register = PythonOperator(task_id="register", python_callable=register_model)

    # dependencies

items.sourcePack: Junior vs Senior — production data engineering
items.title: SQL: full append → incremental idempotent load
items.concept: Junior code often optimizes for getting today’s rows loaded. Senior code defines replay semantics, a business key and a safe state transition.
items.why: Interview lens: How does this behave on reruns, updates, deletes, late arrivals and a table 100× larger?
items.context: Interview questions: How will this handle reruns? What is the watermark? What happens when an order is updated after yesterday’s run?
items.task: Read the Junior baseline in Code. Then open Compare and identify the production guarantees added by the Senior version.
items.starter:
-- JUNIOR: valid for a simple append-only daily feed
INSERT INTO fact_orders (order_id, customer_id, amount, updated_at)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, updated_at
FROM staging_orders
WHERE CAST(updated_at AS date) = CAST(GETDATE() AS date);
items.solution:
-- SENIOR: replay-safe incremental upsert
WITH source_batch AS (
    SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, updated_at,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY order_id
               ORDER BY updated_at DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM staging_orders
    WHERE updated_at >= @watermark_from
      AND updated_at <  @watermark_to
)
MERGE fact_orders AS t
USING (SELECT * FROM source_batch WHERE rn = 1) AS s
   ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at >= t.updated_at THEN
  UPDATE SET customer_id = s.customer_id,
             amount = s.amount,
             updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (order_id, customer_id, amount, updated_at)
  VALUES (s.order_id, s.customer_id, s.amount, s.updated_at);
items.solutionExplanation: The senior version makes the load bounded, deduplicates a business key, tolerates replay and updates only when the incoming version is at least as recent. In production you would advance the watermark only after validation succeeds.
hints: Look for a deterministic business key.
A rerun should converge to the same final state.
Watermark state should advance only after a successful publish.
items.pitfall: A date-only append can duplicate reruns and miss updates that arrive after the original processing date.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  S[Source changes] --> W[Watermark / CDC]
  W --> T[Stage batch]
  T --> D[Deduplicate]
  D --> M[MERGE / upsert]
  M --> Q[Quality + reconciliation]
  Q --> A[Audit watermark]

items.sourcePack: Junior vs Senior — production data engineering
items.title: SQL: DISTINCT → deterministic latest-record dedupe
items.concept: DISTINCT removes byte-identical rows. Production deduplication usually chooses one winner per business key using explicit ordering.
items.why: A senior answer states the key, tie-breaker and audit behavior instead of saying “just use DISTINCT”.
items.context: Interview questions: Which row wins? What if updated_at ties? How do you prove no business key is duplicated afterward?
items.task: Compare the two approaches and explain why the senior query is deterministic for duplicate order events.
items.starter:
-- JUNIOR: useful only when duplicate rows are truly identical
SELECT DISTINCT
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    amount,
    updated_at
FROM raw_orders;
items.solution:
-- SENIOR: choose one winner per business key
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY order_id
               ORDER BY updated_at DESC, ingestion_id DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM raw_orders
)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, updated_at
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
items.solutionExplanation: The senior query defines business-key uniqueness and a deterministic winner. The extra ingestion_id tie-breaker prevents nondeterministic results when source timestamps collide.
hints: ROW_NUMBER needs both a partition key and an ordering rule.
items.pitfall: Ordering only by a non-unique timestamp can still produce nondeterministic winners.

items.sourcePack: Junior vs Senior — production data engineering
items.title: Python: load everything → bounded batch ingestion
items.concept: Junior scripts often materialize every file at once. Senior control code bounds memory, validates inputs and makes failures observable.
items.why: The goal is not clever Python; it is predictable behavior when the file count grows and one file is malformed.
items.context: Interview questions: What happens with 20,000 files? How do you retry one batch? Where do rejected files go?
items.task: Compare the simple pandas load with a batch-oriented version and identify the scalability/recovery differences.
items.starter:
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

paths = list(Path('landing').glob('*.parquet'))
df = pd.concat([pd.read_parquet(path) for path in paths])
df.to_parquet('silver/orders.parquet')
items.solutionExplanation: The senior version bounds the working set, sorts input paths for repeatability, validates the batch before publishing and writes deterministic batch outputs that can be retried independently.
hints: Bound the number of files handled together.
Deterministic ordering makes reruns easier to reason about.
items.pitfall: Batching alone is not idempotency; output naming and publish semantics also need to be deterministic.

items.sourcePack: Junior vs Senior — production data engineering
items.title: Python: one GET → resilient paginated ingestion
items.concept: Production API ingestion needs timeouts, bounded retries, status validation, pagination and a checkpoint.
items.why: A request that works once on a laptop is not yet a reliable ingestion pipeline.
items.context: Interview questions: Which failures are retryable? How do you resume page 438? How do you avoid an infinite pagination loop?
items.task: Compare the short API call with a bounded, observable pagination loop.
items.starter:
import requests

rows = requests.get('https://api.example.com/orders').json()
print(len(rows))
items.solution:
import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry

session = requests.Session()
retry = Retry(
    total=4,
    backoff_factor=1,
    status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],
    allowed_methods=['GET'],
)
session.mount('https://', HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))

page = 1
while True:
    response = session.get(
        'https://api.example.com/orders',
        params={'page': page, 'page_size': 500},
        timeout=(5, 30),
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    payload = response.json()
    rows = payload['items']
    if not rows:
        break
    write_page_idempotently(page, rows)
    save_checkpoint(page)
    page += 1
items.solutionExplanation: The senior version retries only GET requests for transient statuses, uses explicit connection/read timeouts, validates HTTP failures, pages deterministically and checkpoints only after an idempotent write.
hints: Never leave network calls without a timeout.
Retrying POST blindly can duplicate side effects.
items.pitfall: Retries without idempotent writes can make correctness worse rather than better.

items.sourcePack: Junior vs Senior — production data engineering
items.title: PySpark: blind join → size-aware join plan
items.concept: Spark performance is dominated by data movement. Senior code reduces columns/rows early and chooses a join strategy from table size and skew.
items.why: Interview lens: Where is the shuffle? Which side is small? Are keys skewed? What will happen at 100× data volume?
items.context: orders is a multi-terabyte fact; customers is a small dimension. Only paid orders and three fact columns are needed.
items.task: Compare the correct but naive join with a plan that reduces shuffle and data volume.
items.starter:
result = (
    orders
    .join(customers, on='customer_id', how='left')
    .filter("status = 'PAID'")
    .groupBy('country')
    .sum('amount')
)
items.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

paid = (
    orders
    .filter(F.col('status') == 'PAID')
    .select('customer_id', 'amount', 'order_date')
)

dim = customers.select('customer_id', 'country')

result = (
    paid
    .join(F.broadcast(dim), on='customer_id', how='left')
    .groupBy('country')
    .agg(F.sum('amount').alias('revenue'))
)
items.solutionExplanation: The senior version filters and projects the large fact before the join and broadcasts the genuinely small dimension, avoiding a large-side shuffle. A senior answer also says broadcast must be justified by real size/statistics rather than habit.
hints: Filter/select the large side as early as possible.
Broadcast only when the dimension really fits worker memory.
items.pitfall: Forcing broadcast on a large or unexpectedly growing dimension can cause executor memory failures.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  F[Large fact] --> P[Filter + select early]
  D[Small dimension] --> B[Broadcast]
  P --> J[Join]
  B --> J
  J --> G[Aggregate]
  G --> M[Delta MERGE]

items.sourcePack: Junior vs Senior — production data engineering
items.title: PySpark: append → dedupe + Delta MERGE
items.concept: Appending every micro-batch is simple. A senior design defines event identity and converges repeated or updated events into one target state.
items.why: This combines distributed deduplication, idempotent writes and incremental lakehouse processing.
items.context: order_id is the business key. update_ts defines recency. The same source event can be delivered more than once.
items.task: Compare append-only output with a deduplicated Delta MERGE.
items.starter:
(
    incoming
    .write
    .format('delta')
    .mode('append')
    .saveAsTable('silver.orders')
)
items.solution:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

w = Window.partitionBy('order_id').orderBy(F.col('update_ts').desc())
batch = (
    incoming
    .withColumn('_rn', F.row_number().over(w))
    .filter(F.col('_rn') == 1)
    .drop('_rn')
)

target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, 'silver.orders')
(
    target.alias('t')
    .merge(batch.alias('s'), 't.order_id = s.order_id')
    .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition='s.update_ts >= t.update_ts')
    .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
    .execute()
)
items.solutionExplanation: The senior version first picks one source winner per key, then upserts only newer/equal versions. That makes duplicate delivery and reruns converge toward the same target state.
items.pitfall: MERGE is not automatically correct if the source contains multiple rows for the same target key.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  S[Source changes] --> W[Watermark / CDC]
  W --> T[Stage batch]
  T --> D[Deduplicate]
  D --> M[MERGE / upsert]
  M --> Q[Quality + reconciliation]
  Q --> A[Audit watermark]

    .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
    .execute()
)
original.solutionExplanation: The senior version first picks one source winner per key, then upserts only newer/equal versions. That makes duplicate delivery and reruns converge toward the same target state.
original.pitfall: MERGE is not automatically correct if the source contains multiple rows for the same target key.
original.diagram:
flowchart LR
  S[Source changes] --> W[Watermark / CDC]
  W --> T[Stage batch]
  T --> D[Deduplicate]
  D --> M[MERGE / upsert]
  M --> Q[Quality + reconciliation]
  Q --> A[Audit watermark]

items.sourcePack: Junior vs Senior — production data engineering
items.title: dbt: strict max watermark → late-data lookback
items.concept: A strict max(updated_at) predicate is efficient but can permanently miss late-arriving records. Senior incremental logic deliberately re-reads a bounded lookback.
items.why: dbt interviews often test whether you understand incremental materialization beyond copying is_incremental().
items.context: Events can arrive 48 hours late. order_id is unique. The model is rebuilt many times per day.
items.task: Compare the two incremental predicates and explain the correctness/cost trade-off.
items.solutionExplanation: The senior model declares the unique key and merge semantics, then trades a small reprocessing window for protection against late-arriving updates. The correct lookback length should come from observed lateness/SLA data.
hints: A lookback intentionally reprocesses some already-seen rows.
Reprocessing is safe only when the write is idempotent.
items.pitfall: A lookback without a unique key/merge can simply create duplicates faster.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SRC[source()] --> STG[staging]
  STG --> INT[intermediate]
  INT --> MART[mart]
  MART --> TEST[tests]
  MART --> DOC[docs / lineage]
  TEST --> DEPLOY[CI / deploy]

items.sourcePack: Junior vs Senior — production data engineering
items.title: Data quality: assert → quarantine + reconciliation
items.concept: An assertion is useful during development. Production quality design decides what fails the pipeline, what is quarantined and what is measured.
items.why: Senior engineers make bad-data behavior explicit so downstream consumers know whether a dataset is safe to use.
items.context: Required: order_id non-null, amount >= 0. Invalid rows should not enter Silver but should remain diagnosable.
items.task: Compare the one-line assertion with an explicit valid/invalid split and reconciliation metric.
items.starter:
assert df['order_id'].notna().all()
assert (df['amount'] >= 0).all()
write_silver(df)
items.solution:
valid_mask = df['order_id'].notna() & df['amount'].ge(0)
valid = df.loc[valid_mask].copy()
invalid = df.loc[~valid_mask].copy()

metrics = {
    'input_rows': len(df),
    'valid_rows': len(valid),
    'invalid_rows': len(invalid),
}
assert metrics['input_rows'] == metrics['valid_rows'] + metrics['invalid_rows']

write_quarantine(invalid)
write_silver_idempotently(valid)
publish_quality_metrics(metrics)
items.solutionExplanation: The senior version preserves rejected evidence, reconciles input/valid/invalid counts and makes publication behavior explicit. Whether invalid rows should stop the whole pipeline depends on the contract and business criticality.
hints: Reconcile counts at a boundary before publishing.
items.pitfall: Silently dropping invalid records creates “clean” tables with unmeasured data loss.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  I[Ingest] --> C{Contract checks}
  C -->|valid| S[Silver]
  C -->|invalid| Q[Quarantine]
  S --> R[Reconciliation]
  R --> P[Publish]
  Q --> O[Metrics / alert]

items.title: Source lab: create an RDD with parallelize
items.concept: An RDD is a partitioned distributed collection. Modern PySpark usually prefers DataFrames, but RDDs explain Spark’s execution model.
items.why: Know the abstraction, then know why DataFrame APIs are generally preferred for structured data.
items.context: Uploaded course · 2-novice/1-Initiation-RDD.ipynb · create values from 1..n with SparkContext.parallelize.
items.task: Return an RDD containing integers from 1 through n.
items.solution:
def rdd_from_list(sc, n):
    return sc.parallelize(range(1, n + 1))
items.pitfall: Do not collect large RDDs back to the driver just to inspect them.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  D[Driver] --> R[RDD]
  R --> P1[Partition 1]
  R --> P2[Partition 2]
  R --> P3[Partition 3]
  P1 --> T[Transformations]
  P2 --> T
  P3 --> T
  T --> A[Action / result]

items.title: Source lab: map + filter without collecting
items.concept: Transformations such as map and filter are lazy; they describe distributed work until an action or write executes it.
items.why: Interviewers expect you to distinguish transformations, actions and driver-side materialization.
items.context: Use an RDD of CSV lines after removing the header. Keep Residential rows and return policy IDs.
items.task: Filter Residential records and map each remaining row to its policyID.
items.starter:
residential_ids = (
    rows
    # filter Residential rows
    # map to policyID
)
items.solution:
residential_ids = (
    rows
    .filter(lambda line: ',Residential,' in line)
    .map(lambda line: line.split(',')[0])
)
hints: policyID is the first CSV field.
items.pitfall: Parsing production CSV with split(",") is fragile; this drill mirrors the RDD course, while DataFrame csv readers are preferable for structured files.

items.title: Source lab: aggregate insurance value by construction
items.concept: DataFrame groupBy + agg is a wide transformation: data with the same key must be brought together.
items.why: The syntax is easy; the senior question is where the shuffle happens and how many groups/rows move.
items.context: FL insurance sample · compare total tiv_2012 by construction for Residential policies.
items.task: Filter Residential rows, group by construction and sum tiv_2012 as total_tiv_2012.
items.starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

result = (
    df
    # filter
    # group
    # aggregate
)
items.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

result = (
    df
    .filter(F.col('line') == 'Residential')
    .groupBy('construction')
    .agg(F.sum('tiv_2012').alias('total_tiv_2012'))
)
items.pitfall: groupBy causes a shuffle; do not add unnecessary repartitions around it.

items.title: Source lab: keep toPandas at a safe boundary
items.concept: toPandas collects the entire Spark DataFrame into driver memory.
items.why: The uploaded tutorial explicitly warns to use toPandas only for small DataFrames; this is a common real-world failure mode.
items.context: You need a small 20-row summary for plotting, not the full fact table.
items.task: Aggregate in Spark, limit the result and only then convert the small summary to pandas.
items.starter:
pdf = large_fact.toPandas()
summary = pdf.groupby('county')['amount'].sum()
items.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

summary = (
    large_fact
    .groupBy('county')
    .agg(F.sum('amount').alias('revenue'))
    .orderBy(F.col('revenue').desc())
    .limit(20)
)
pdf = summary.toPandas()
hints: Reduce rows and columns before crossing to the driver.
items.pitfall: A full toPandas can crash the driver even when the Spark cluster has plenty of aggregate memory.

items.title: Optional NoSQL: Redis query cache
items.concept: Redis is an in-memory key/value system commonly used for low-latency caching and ephemeral state.
items.why: Useful breadth, but not a replacement for core relational modeling skills.
items.context: Uploaded Redis notebook models a REST query cache identified by HTTP method + URL.
items.task: Cache a JSON response for GET /customers/42 with a 60-second TTL.
items.starter:
import redis, json
r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379)
key = # method + url
# store response with expiry
items.solution:
import redis, json
r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379)
key = 'GET:/customers/42'
r.setex(key, 60, json.dumps({'customer_id': 42, 'status': 'active'}))
items.pitfall: A cache needs an invalidation/TTL strategy; stale cached data is a correctness problem.

movies = db.movies
cursor = movies.find(

movies = db.movies
cursor = movies.find(

items.title: Optional GenAI: embeddings + cosine similarity
items.concept: An embedding maps text to a vector so semantic relatedness can be approximated with vector similarity.
items.why: This is enough foundation to understand vector search without turning the DE trainer into an AI course.
items.context: Uploaded GenAI tutorial uses SentenceTransformers and cosine similarity between sentence embeddings.
items.task: Encode three sentences and compute similarity between the first two.
items.starter:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util
model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')
sentences = ['red cat', 'my red cat', 'warehouse partitioning']
# encode and compare
items.solution:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util
model = SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2')
sentences = ['red cat', 'my red cat', 'warehouse partitioning']
emb = model.encode(sentences)
score = util.cos_sim(emb[0], emb[1]).item()
items.pitfall: Embedding similarity is not a factuality guarantee and depends heavily on model/domain.

items.title: Optional GenAI: local OpenAI-compatible endpoint
items.concept: Local runtimes can expose an OpenAI-compatible API, letting application code swap providers with minimal interface changes.
items.why: Useful for privacy/testing, but operational concerns like model memory, latency and versioning remain.
items.context: Uploaded tutorial demonstrates LMStudio/Ollama-style local endpoints.
items.task: Create a client pointing at a local endpoint and send one chat request.
items.starter:
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(
    base_url=#,
    api_key='local',
)
# request
items.solution:
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(
    base_url='http://localhost:11434/v1',
    api_key='ollama',
)
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model='mistral',
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Summarize this data-quality incident.'}],
)
hints: Point base_url at the local compatible server.
items.pitfall: API compatibility does not mean model capability, context limits or structured-output behavior are identical.

items.title: Optional K8s: ConfigMap vs Secret
items.concept: Configuration belongs outside the image; non-secret settings and credentials have different handling requirements.
items.why: The important DE lesson is separation of code/config/secrets, not memorizing every Kubernetes resource.
items.context: Inject API_NAME from a ConfigMap and API_KEY from a Secret into a container.
items.task: Complete the two env valueFrom references.
items.starter:
env:
  - name: API_NAME
    valueFrom:
      # config map reference
  - name: API_KEY
    valueFrom:
      # secret reference
items.solution:
env:
  - name: API_NAME
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: api-config
        key: API_NAME
  - name: API_KEY
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: api-secrets
        key: api-key
hints: ConfigMapKeyRef and SecretKeyRef are separate references.
items.pitfall: A Kubernetes Secret is not magically safe merely because it is called Secret; use proper RBAC/encryption/external secret management in real environments.

items.title: File format vs table format vs engine
items.concept: Parquet, Avro and JSON encode files/records. Delta Lake adds table-level transaction semantics. DuckDB is a query engine/database.
items.why: Interview answers become confusing when these layers are treated as interchangeable products.
items.context: Classify: Parquet · Avro · JSON · Delta Lake · DuckDB.
items.task: Place each technology in the correct layer and give one primary use case.
items.starter:
FILE FORMAT:
- 

TABLE FORMAT / TRANSACTION LAYER:
- 

QUERY ENGINE / DATABASE:
-
items.solution:
FILE FORMAT:
- Parquet — columnar analytical files
- Avro — row-oriented schema-aware records
- JSON — flexible semi-structured interchange

TABLE FORMAT / TRANSACTION LAYER:
- Delta Lake — table metadata/transactions over data files

QUERY ENGINE / DATABASE:
- DuckDB — in-process analytical SQL engine
hints: Ask whether the technology describes bytes in a file, table transactions/metadata, or query execution.
items.pitfall: Delta Lake is not just a Parquet replacement codec, and DuckDB is not a file format.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  J[JSON / Avro landing] --> S[Transform]
  S --> P[Parquet data files]
  P --> D[Delta table layer]
  D --> E[PySpark / SQL engine]
  P --> U[DuckDB / Python local analytics]

original.starter:
FILE FORMAT:
-

- 

QUERY ENGINE / DATABASE:
-
original.solution:
FILE FORMAT:
- Parquet — columnar analytical files
- Avro — row-oriented schema-aware records
- JSON — flexible semi-structured interchange

TABLE FORMAT / TRANSACTION LAYER:
- Delta Lake — table metadata/transactions over data files

QUERY ENGINE / DATABASE:
- DuckDB — in-process analytical SQL engine

items.title: Read Parquet efficiently in pandas
items.concept: Parquet readers can project only required columns; avoid loading wide tables when the task uses three fields.
items.why: Reducing bytes read is often a larger win than micro-optimizing Python code.
items.context: orders.parquet has order_id, customer_id, amount, status, event_date and many unused columns.
items.task: Read only order_id, customer_id, amount and event_date with pandas.
items.starter:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_parquet(
    'orders.parquet',
    columns=#
)
items.solution:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_parquet(
    'orders.parquet',
    columns=['order_id', 'customer_id', 'amount', 'event_date'],
    engine='pyarrow',
)
hints: pyarrow is a common pandas Parquet engine.
items.pitfall: Reading every column and dropping most of them afterwards wastes I/O and memory.

items.title: Filter a Parquet dataset with PyArrow
items.concept: PyArrow Dataset can express column projection and filters at the dataset scan layer.
items.why: This exposes the same pruning/pushdown ideas used by larger analytical engines.
items.context: lake/orders contains partitioned Parquet files. Need customer_id + amount for event_date >= 2026-09-01.
items.task: Create a dataset scan with two selected columns and an event_date filter.
items.starter:
import pyarrow.dataset as ds

dataset = ds.dataset('lake/orders', format='parquet')
table = dataset.to_table(
    columns=#,
    filter=#,
)
items.solution:
import pyarrow.dataset as ds

dataset = ds.dataset('lake/orders', format='parquet')
table = dataset.to_table(
    columns=['customer_id', 'amount'],
    filter=ds.field('event_date') >= '2026-09-01',
)
items.pitfall: A Python filter after table.to_pandas() happens too late to reduce the original scan.

items.title: Read and write Parquet with PySpark
items.concept: Spark reads Parquet natively and can combine projection, filters and partitioned writes in a distributed plan.
items.why: This is a standard lake ingestion/curation pattern in Databricks and Fabric Spark.
items.context: Read /lake/orders, keep four columns, filter recent dates, then write partitioned by event_date.
items.task: Complete the PySpark read/transform/write chain.
items.starter:
df = (spark.read
    .#('/lake/orders')
    .select(#)
    .filter(#))

(df.write.mode('append')
   .partitionBy(#)
   .parquet('/lake/orders_curated'))
items.solution:
df = (spark.read
    .parquet('/lake/orders')
    .select('order_id', 'customer_id', 'amount', 'event_date')
    .filter("event_date >= '2026-09-01'"))

(df.write.mode('append')
   .partitionBy('event_date')
   .parquet('/lake/orders_curated'))
hints: Use a coarse reporting/filter key for the example partition.
items.pitfall: Do not partition by a nearly unique business key such as order_id.

items.title: Query Parquet directly with DuckDB
items.concept: DuckDB can query analytical files directly without loading them into a server database first.
items.why: It is useful for local validation, ad-hoc analytics and testing lake transformations.
items.context: lake/orders/*.parquet contains customer_id, amount, event_date.
items.task: Return revenue by customer for events from 2026-09-01 onward.
items.starter:
SELECT #
FROM read_parquet('lake/orders/*.parquet')
WHERE #
GROUP BY #;
items.solution:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM read_parquet('lake/orders/*.parquet')
WHERE event_date >= DATE '2026-09-01'
GROUP BY customer_id;
hints: Project only the group key and aggregate.
items.pitfall: DuckDB is the engine executing SQL over Parquet; Parquet itself does not execute queries.

items.title: Normalize nested JSON in Python
items.concept: JSON is convenient for semi-structured interchange, but analytics often need explicit normalization and types.
items.why: Bronze/API data frequently arrives as nested JSON before being curated to a columnar format.
items.context: records contains nested customer objects and line items.
items.task: Normalize records to a tabular DataFrame while retaining order_id and nested customer fields.
items.starter:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.json_normalize(
    records,
    # configure nested/meta fields
)
items.solution:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.json_normalize(
    records,
    record_path='items',
    meta=['order_id', ['customer', 'customer_id'], ['customer', 'country']],
    errors='ignore',
)
hints: record_path identifies the repeated child array.
meta carries parent fields into each normalized row.
items.pitfall: Flexible JSON does not remove the need for a downstream schema/data contract.

items.title: Choose a safe partition key
items.concept: Partitioning is coarse physical organization used to skip unrelated data. Very high-cardinality keys can create pathological file/directory counts.
items.why: Bad partition design is a common lake performance and operational failure mode.
items.context: orders has 5 years of data, 40 million customer_id values, 25 regions and daily reporting filters.
items.task: Choose a partition key and explain why customer_id is a poor default partition key.
items.starter:
# choose one
partition_key = # 'event_date' | 'region' | 'customer_id'
reason = #
items.solution:
partition_key = 'event_date'
reason = 'Daily/date filtering is common and cardinality is bounded. customer_id is too high-cardinality for directory-style partitioning; region may be useful in combination with workload-specific clustering/layout.'
hints: Prefer common pruning predicates with manageable cardinality.
Unique IDs usually make poor directory partitions.
items.pitfall: More partitions are not automatically more parallel or faster.
items.diagram:
flowchart TD
  Q[Query filter] --> A{Coarse common key?}
  A -->|Yes| P[Partition pruning]
  A -->|No / additional filters| C[Clustering / data locality]
  C --> I{Database point/range access?}
  I -->|Yes| X[Index]
  I -->|No| F[Column pruning + pushdown]
  P --> F
  X --> F

items.title: Partitioning vs clustering
items.concept: Clustering is an engine/table-format-specific way to colocate similar values so scans can skip more data without one partition per value.
items.why: Clustering is often useful for secondary high-value filters that are too granular for coarse partitioning.
items.context: The table is partitioned by event_date but often filtered by customer_id.
items.task: Explain a reasonable layout and state that clustering syntax/behavior is engine-specific.
items.starter:
-- conceptual design
PARTITION BY #
CLUSTER BY #
items.solution:
-- conceptual design (exact DDL is engine-specific)
PARTITION BY event_date
CLUSTER BY customer_id

-- The partition provides coarse date pruning; clustering improves locality/data skipping for customer filters without creating one partition per customer.
hints: Treat exact clustering syntax as platform-specific.
items.pitfall: Do not confuse a SQL Server clustered index, BigQuery clustering and Delta/Databricks clustering as identical implementations.

items.title: Design a useful SQL index
items.concept: A B-tree-style index provides ordered lookup paths. Composite key order and included columns should match real predicates and projections.
items.why: Database indexes are central for OLTP/relational query tuning but are different from lake partitioning.
items.context: Most queries filter customer_id = ? and order_date between ? and ?, then return amount and status.
items.task: Create a SQL Server nonclustered index that supports the access pattern.
hints: Put equality/range search columns in the key.
Return-only columns can be INCLUDE columns in SQL Server.
items.pitfall: Every index adds storage and write-maintenance cost; more indexes are not free.

items.title: Fix the small-file problem
items.concept: Many tiny analytical files create metadata, listing, file-open and scheduling overhead even when total bytes are modest.
items.why: The small-file problem is a frequent Spark/lakehouse performance issue.
items.context: A daily batch writes 80,000 tiny files for 100 GB of data.
items.task: Reduce output file count deliberately before the batch write and explain why one giant file is also not ideal.
items.starter:
target_partitions = #
out = df.#(target_partitions, 'event_date')
(out.write
   .partitionBy('event_date')
   .parquet(path))
items.solution:
target_partitions = 128  # choose from measured data size/cluster/workload, not as a universal constant
out = df.repartition(target_partitions, 'event_date')
(out.write
   .mode('append')
   .partitionBy('event_date')
   .parquet(path))

# For Delta/lakehouse systems, scheduled compaction/OPTIMIZE can consolidate files after ingestion where supported.
hints: Control partitions/files using measured workload characteristics.
Compaction is often separate from low-latency ingestion.
items.pitfall: Hard-coding 128 as universally correct would be another tuning bug; file sizing is workload/platform dependent.

items.title: Pruning, pushdown and column projection
items.concept: Partition pruning skips partitions, predicate pushdown moves eligible filters to the scan, and column pruning avoids reading unused columns.
items.why: These optimizations reduce bytes read before expensive joins/aggregations happen.
items.context: A Parquet lake has 120 columns and 5 years of date partitions. The report needs 3 columns for one week.
items.task: Write a narrow query and explain the three distinct pruning mechanisms an engine may apply.
items.solution:
SELECT customer_id, event_date, amount
FROM read_parquet('lake/events/**/*.parquet')
WHERE event_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-09-01' AND DATE '2026-09-07';

-- column pruning: only 3 columns
-- partition pruning: skip unrelated date partitions when partition metadata/layout is available
-- predicate pushdown: apply eligible event_date filtering at the scan/reader level
hints: Use EXPLAIN/query plans to verify optimizations rather than assuming them.
items.pitfall: A WHERE clause expresses semantics; it is not proof that a specific source reader actually pushed the predicate down.

items.title: Choose compression by workload
items.concept: Compression trades CPU for lower storage and I/O. Analytical formats compress especially well column-by-column.
items.why: The smallest file is not automatically the fastest end-to-end pipeline.
items.context: Compare Snappy and a denser codec for a large Parquet dataset.
items.task: Write Parquet with Snappy and state the three metrics you would benchmark before changing codecs.
items.starter:
df.write.option('compression', #).parquet(path)
metrics = [#, #, #]
items.solution:
df.write.option('compression', 'snappy').parquet(path)
metrics = ['file_size', 'write_time', 'scan_time']
hints: Measure both storage and compute/I/O performance.
items.pitfall: Codec support and optimal choice vary by engine and workload; benchmark instead of assuming.

items.title: Triage a broken ETL pipeline
items.concept: Locate the first stage where a known invariant becomes false.
items.why: Randomly changing code is slower than proving where the failure begins.
items.context: Source → ingest → Bronze → transform → Gold → report.
items.task: Write the seven-step incident workflow from symptom to prevention.
items.starter:
1. Symptom:
2. First bad stage:
3. Evidence:
4. Hypothesis:
5. Safe fix:
6. Replay:
7. Prevention:
items.solution:
1. Confirm symptom/business impact
2. Find first bad stage
3. Gather logs/counts/keys/schema/plan/timestamps
4. Test one hypothesis
5. Fix safely
6. Replay/backfill idempotently
7. Reconcile and add prevention checks
items.pitfall: Restarting everything can destroy useful evidence.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  S[Source] --> I[Ingest]
  I --> B[Bronze]
  B --> T[Transform]
  T --> G[Gold]
  G --> R[Report / consumer]
  I -. schema/auth/network .-> F[Failure evidence]
  T -. bad join / null / skew .-> F
  G -. duplicate / missing partition .-> F
  F --> C[Counts + keys + schema + logs + plan]
  C --> X[Safe fix]
  X --> P[Replay / backfill]
  P --> V[Reconcile + prevention test]

items.title: Find missing rows with reconciliation SQL
items.concept: Counts and anti-joins locate loss between source and target.
items.why: A row-count mismatch should be explained with concrete keys.
items.context: source_orders should be represented in target_orders by order_id.
items.task: Return source order_ids missing from target.
items.starter:
SELECT s.order_id
FROM source_orders s
-- join target_orders
-- keep missing target rows
items.solution:
SELECT s.order_id
FROM source_orders s
LEFT JOIN target_orders t
  ON s.order_id = t.order_id
WHERE t.order_id IS NULL;
hints: Missing target keys have NULL on t.
items.pitfall: COUNT(*) alone tells you size, not which business keys disappeared.

items.title: Fix duplicate rows after a rerun
items.concept: Retries/backfills need idempotent target writes.
items.why: Append-only reruns can duplicate every business event.
items.context: stage_orders contains updates keyed by order_id.
items.task: Use MERGE logic so rerunning the same data converges to one row per order_id.
items.starter:
MERGE INTO target_orders t
USING stage_orders s
ON -- key
WHEN MATCHED THEN --
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN --;
items.solution:
MERGE INTO target_orders t
USING stage_orders s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET amount = s.amount, updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (order_id, amount, updated_at) VALUES (s.order_id, s.amount, s.updated_at);
items.pitfall: Deleting the whole table before every retry can create larger outages.

items.title: Recover late data beyond a watermark
items.concept: A strict MAX(timestamp) checkpoint can permanently miss late arrivals.
items.why: Distributed sources rarely guarantee perfect arrival order.
items.context: Target max_loaded_at is 2026-09-03; a valid record updated on 2026-09-02 arrived today.
items.task: Use a two-day lookback and rely on idempotent dedupe/upsert downstream.
items.starter:
SELECT * FROM source
WHERE updated_at >= -- lookback
items.solution:
SELECT * FROM source
WHERE updated_at >= max_loaded_at - INTERVAL '2 days';
items.pitfall: Lookback without deterministic dedupe/upsert can create duplicates.

items.title: Debug a missing daily partition
items.concept: Missing data can be a path/date/timezone problem rather than a transformation bug.
items.why: Partition routing bugs are common around UTC/local-date boundaries.
items.context: The job succeeded, but event_date=2026-09-03 is empty.
items.task: List the checks in order: source date/timezone, generated partition key, target path, file count, pruning predicate.
items.solution:
CHECKS:
1. Confirm source event timestamps and timezone
2. Recompute expected partition key
3. Inspect target partition/path existence
4. Count/list files and rows in neighboring partitions
5. Verify query partition predicate/pruning
items.pitfall: Re-running blindly can write the same bad partition key again.

items.title: Diagnose a many-to-many join explosion
items.concept: Unexpected duplicate keys on both join sides multiply rows.
items.why: Join explosions corrupt metrics and can also cause memory/shuffle failures.
items.context: orders should join many-to-one with customers.
items.task: Find customer_id values duplicated in the supposed customer dimension.
items.starter:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) n
FROM customers
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING --
items.solution:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) n
FROM customers
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
hints: Validate dimension uniqueness before the join.
items.pitfall: Adding DISTINCT after the join can hide the real grain problem.

items.title: Redesign bad high-cardinality partitioning
items.concept: Partitioning should support coarse pruning without creating huge metadata/file counts.
items.why: Partitioning by nearly unique IDs creates tiny partitions and slow listing/planning.
items.context: 4 TB orders are partitioned by customer_id; most queries filter date and region.
items.task: Propose a better physical layout and explain where clustering could help.
items.starter:
PARTITION BY:
CLUSTER / DATA SKIP BY:
WHY:
items.solution:
PARTITION BY: event_date (or another coarse common date key)
CLUSTER / DATA SKIP BY: region and/or customer_id where the platform supports it
WHY: date pruning removes large ranges while clustering helps secondary filters without millions of partitions
items.pitfall: More partitions are not automatically more parallel or faster.

items.title: Fix a small-file pipeline
items.concept: Many tiny files create listing, metadata and task overhead.
items.why: A pipeline can become slower even when total data volume is unchanged.
items.context: A micro-batch writes one small Parquet file per minute per partition.
items.task: Describe a safer strategy: controlled repartition/coalesce, target file sizing and periodic compaction.
items.starter:
# before write
out = df.________(64, "event_date")
# write partitioned
# schedule compaction
items.solution:
# before write
out = df.repartition(64, "event_date")
(out.write.mode("append")
   .partitionBy("event_date")
   .parquet(path))
# Periodically compact old partitions to an appropriate target file size.
items.pitfall: Coalescing everything to one file creates a different bottleneck.

items.title: Detect a skewed Spark join key
items.concept: One hot key can create a straggler partition that dominates job duration.
items.why: Adding more executors rarely fixes a single badly skewed key.
items.context: One join task takes 25 minutes while most finish in 30 seconds.
items.task: Show the most frequent join keys.
items.starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

(df.groupBy("customer_id")
   .count()
   .________(F.desc("count"))
   .show(20))
items.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

(df.groupBy("customer_id")
   .count()
   .orderBy(F.desc("count"))
   .show(20))
items.pitfall: Blind repartitioning does not remove a genuinely hot key.

items.title: Debug Spark driver OOM from collect/toPandas
items.concept: collect() and toPandas() move distributed data to the driver.
items.why: A cluster can have plenty of executor memory while the driver still crashes.
items.context: The job succeeds until a final df.toPandas() on 80 GB.
items.task: Replace the driver collection with a distributed write or bounded sample.
items.starter:
# bad
pdf = df.toPandas()

# safer
# ...
items.solution:
# distributed output
df.write.mode("overwrite").parquet(output_path)

# bounded inspection only
sample_pdf = df.limit(1000).toPandas()
items.pitfall: Increasing driver memory only postpones an unbounded collection problem.

items.title: Fix an Airflow retry storm
items.concept: Airflow retry policy belongs to the failure mode, not a global default.
items.why: Bad-data tasks that retry repeatedly consume worker/pool capacity and delay healthy DAGs.
items.context: A validation task retries 10 times for a deterministic schema mismatch.
items.task: Set validation to fail once while the API extraction task keeps bounded retries/backoff.
hints: Validation errors are deterministic; network errors may be transient.
items.pitfall: A large retry count can become an outage multiplier.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Schedule / dataset event] --> E[Extract]
  E --> Q{Validate input}
  Q -->|good| T[Transform]
  Q -->|bad deterministic data| D[Quarantine / fail once]
  T --> L[Load idempotently]
  L --> V[Reconcile]
  V --> P[Publish]
  E -. timeout / 429 / 5xx .-> R[Bounded retry + backoff]
  R --> E
  T -. transient infra error .-> R

items.title: Debug an Airflow task stuck queued
items.concept: Queued tasks often indicate scheduler/executor/pool/concurrency capacity rather than task-code failure.
items.why: Reading only the task log may show nothing because the task has not started.
items.context: Workers are healthy, but a task remains queued for 40 minutes.
items.task: List five orchestration checks before changing task code.
items.solution:
1. Pool and pool-slot availability
2. DAG/task concurrency and max active runs
3. Executor/worker slots and queue health
4. Scheduler health/heartbeat and executor communication
5. Upstream dependencies, priority/queue routing and resource requests

items.title: Design a safe 90-day backfill
items.concept: Backfills should be bounded, idempotent, observable and reconciled before scaling concurrency.
items.why: A large catchup can overload sources, clusters and downstream consumers.
items.context: Need to replay 90 historical partitions after correcting a transformation.
items.task: Design a staged backfill sequence.
items.starter:
PHASE 1:
PHASE 2:
PHASE 3:
VALIDATION:
ROLLBACK:
items.solution:
PHASE 1: replay 1-2 partitions in isolation
PHASE 2: reconcile counts/keys/KPIs and verify idempotency
PHASE 3: expand in controlled batches with concurrency limits
VALIDATION: per-partition data-quality + business reconciliation
ROLLBACK: keep old version/partition or transactional restore path until validation passes
hints: Do not start with all 90 days.
items.pitfall: Unbounded catchup can turn a data fix into an infrastructure incident.

    .filter(F.col('amount').isNull() | (F.col('amount') < 0))

items.title: Use Polars lazy execution for a local Parquet pipeline
items.concept: Polars LazyFrame can optimize projection/filtering before execution.
items.why: It is a strong option for local analytical transforms that do not need distributed Spark.
items.context: Compute customer revenue from local Parquet files while reading only necessary data.
items.task: Use scan_parquet, filter, select/group_by and collect.
items.starter:
import polars as pl

result = (pl.scan_parquet('orders/*.parquet')
    # filter/select/group
    .collect())
items.solution:
import polars as pl

result = (
    pl.scan_parquet('orders/*.parquet')
      .filter(pl.col('status') == 'PAID')
      .group_by('customer_id')
      .agg(pl.col('amount').sum().alias('revenue'))
      .collect()
)
hints: scan_parquet is lazy; read_parquet is eager.
items.pitfall: Calling collect too early prevents the optimizer from seeing later operations.

items.title: Use DuckDB as a pipeline validation microscope
items.concept: DuckDB can query local/cloud Parquet quickly without loading it into a separate database first.
items.why: It is useful for ad-hoc reconciliation and debugging small-to-medium lake slices.
items.context: Validate row/key counts by day from produced Parquet.
items.task: Return daily row count, distinct order count and total amount.
items.starter:
SELECT event_date,
       COUNT(*) AS rows,
       -- distinct keys
       -- total amount
FROM read_parquet('lake/orders/*.parquet')
GROUP BY event_date;
items.solution:
SELECT event_date,
       COUNT(*) AS rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS distinct_orders,
       SUM(amount) AS amount
FROM read_parquet('lake/orders/*.parquet')
GROUP BY event_date
ORDER BY event_date;
items.pitfall: For truly distributed multi-terabyte transformations, a local DuckDB process may not be the right execution engine.

items.title: Iceberg hidden partitioning and partition evolution
items.concept: Iceberg supports partition transforms and partition evolution while hiding physical partition layout from normal query predicates.
items.why: It separates logical filtering from a rigid Hive-style directory contract and lets layout evolve without eagerly rewriting old files.
items.context: events(id BIGINT, event_time TIMESTAMP, customer_id BIGINT, payload STRING). Queries filter by event_time and sometimes customer_id.
items.task: Create an Iceberg table using a day transform for event_time and buckets for customer_id, then explain what happens if the partition spec changes later.
items.starter:
CREATE TABLE prod.analytics.events (
  id BIGINT,
  event_time TIMESTAMP,
  customer_id BIGINT,
  payload STRING
)
USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (#);
items.solution:
CREATE TABLE prod.analytics.events (
  id BIGINT,
  event_time TIMESTAMP,
  customer_id BIGINT,
  payload STRING
)
USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (days(event_time), bucket(32, customer_id));

-- Queries still filter logical columns, e.g. event_time.
-- If the partition spec evolves, old and new layouts can coexist;
-- changing the spec is metadata-driven rather than an eager rewrite of all old files.
hints: Iceberg Spark DDL supports transforms such as days(ts), bucket(N, col) and truncate.
Query the logical timestamp column rather than constructing partition directory predicates.
items.pitfall: Hidden partitioning does not mean physical layout is irrelevant; it means users query logical columns while Iceberg handles partition mapping.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Q[WHERE event_time >= ...] --> M[Iceberg metadata]
  M --> A[old partition spec files]
  M --> B[new partition spec files]
  A --> R[matching rows]
  B --> R

items.title: Fabric: separate V-Order from clustering and compaction
items.concept: V-Order is a Fabric write/file-layout optimization for Parquet; compaction reduces small-file overhead; clustering/Z-Order address data locality for selective predicates.
items.why: These optimizations are complementary concepts and should not be described as synonyms.
items.context: A Fabric Delta table has many small files and feeds repeated Power BI/SQL/Spark reads.
items.task: Explain which problem V-Order solves, which problem OPTIMIZE compaction solves, and where a clustering strategy fits.
items.starter:
V-ORDER:
- 

COMPACTION / OPTIMIZE:
- 

CLUSTERING / Z-ORDER:
-
items.solution:
V-ORDER:
- Reorganizes the Parquet file layout at write/maintenance time for efficient Fabric reads.

COMPACTION / OPTIMIZE:
- Consolidates many small files into fewer larger files, reducing metadata/open-file overhead.

CLUSTERING / Z-ORDER:
- Improves data locality/file skipping for frequently filtered columns.

Always benchmark on the actual Fabric runtime/workload because defaults and supported maintenance syntax evolve.
hints: Think file encoding/layout vs file count vs value locality.
items.pitfall: V-Order is not a replacement name for partitioning, Z-Order or liquid clustering.
