items.title: Fabric: partitioning vs liquid clustering
items.concept: Current Fabric Runtime 2.0 guidance favors liquid clustering for most read-performance scenarios, while Hive-style partitioning remains useful when disjoint partitions isolate concurrent writers.
items.why: Choosing layout from query behavior and write concurrency avoids thousands of tiny directories and unnecessary maintenance.
items.context: A sales Delta table is filtered by customer_id and region. Four pipelines concurrently MERGE separate legal entities.
items.task: Choose a physical layout and explain the trade-off between read optimization and writer isolation.
items.starter:
READ PATTERN:

WRITE CONCURRENCY:

LAYOUT CHOICE:

WHY:
items.solution:
READ PATTERN:
- customer_id is high-cardinality, so directory partitioning by customer_id is a poor default.

WRITE CONCURRENCY:
- if each pipeline truly owns a disjoint low/moderate-cardinality legal_entity partition, partitioning can isolate concurrent writes.

LAYOUT CHOICE:
- for read skipping alone on modern Fabric Runtime 2.0, prefer liquid clustering on useful filter columns.
- if concurrent MERGE isolation is the primary need, carefully chosen partitions can still be justified.

items.title: Read a Spark plan through the AQE lens
items.concept: Adaptive Query Execution uses runtime statistics to re-optimize parts of Spark SQL/DataFrame plans, including shuffle partition coalescing and some join/skew decisions.
items.why: Senior Spark tuning is not just setting spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to a magic number.
items.context: A large join is planned as sort-merge, but one side is much smaller after filters and a few shuffle partitions are skewed.
items.task: Enable/verify AQE, inspect the formatted plan, and list three adaptations AQE can make.
items.starter:
spark.conf.set('spark.sql.adaptive.enabled', #)

result = fact.join(dim, 'customer_id')
result.explain(#)

# AQE can:
# 1.
# 2.
# 3.
items.solution:
spark.conf.set('spark.sql.adaptive.enabled', 'true')

result = fact.join(dim, 'customer_id')
result.explain('formatted')

# AQE can, depending on runtime statistics/configuration:
# 1. coalesce post-shuffle partitions
# 2. convert an eligible sort-merge join to a broadcast/hash strategy
# 3. split/mitigate skewed shuffle partitions
hints: Look for adaptive plan information and Exchange/join nodes.
AQE reacts to runtime statistics; it does not excuse bad data modeling or an accidental many-to-many join.
items.pitfall: Do not assume AQE guarantees a specific join conversion; thresholds, statistics and runtime conditions still matter.

items.title: Use Polars lazy Parquet scanning before choosing Spark
items.concept: Polars scan_parquet returns a LazyFrame so the optimizer can push eligible projections and predicates into the scan.
items.why: A local workload may be solved more simply by reducing I/O rather than immediately moving to distributed compute.
items.context: You need daily revenue by customer from a local/cloud Parquet dataset and only three columns are required.
items.task: Build a lazy scan that filters recent rows, selects the needed columns, aggregates revenue, then collects once.
items.starter:
import polars as pl

result = (
    pl.#('orders/*.parquet')
      .filter(#)
      .select(#)
      .group_by('customer_id')
      .agg(#)
      .collect()
)
items.solution:
import polars as pl

result = (
    pl.scan_parquet('orders/*.parquet')
      .filter(pl.col('event_date') >= pl.date(2026, 9, 1))
      .select('customer_id', 'amount', 'event_date')
      .group_by('customer_id')
      .agg(pl.col('amount').sum().alias('revenue'))
      .collect()
)
hints: Use scan_parquet, not read_parquet, for a lazy scan.
Collect at the end of the logical plan.
items.pitfall: Lazy execution is not a promise that every operation will push down; inspect the plan/profile when performance matters.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Parquet workload] --> B{Single machine comfortable?}
  B -->|yes, SQL-first| D[DuckDB]
  B -->|yes, DataFrame/lazy transforms| P[Polars]
  B -->|no / distributed platform standard| S[PySpark]
  D --> M[Measure bytes, memory, latency]
  P --> M
  S --> M

items.title: dbt microbatch for large time-series models
items.concept: dbt microbatch splits a time-series incremental model into bounded event_time batches that can be processed/retried independently.
items.why: It provides a structured alternative to hand-written max(timestamp) incremental logic for supported adapters and appropriate time-series models.
items.context: events is large, append-heavy and keyed by event_occurred_at. Late rows can arrive up to three daily batches late.
items.task: Configure a daily microbatch model with a three-batch lookback and a fixed begin date.
items.solution:
{{ config(
  materialized='incremental',
  incremental_strategy='microbatch',
  event_time='event_occurred_at',
  begin='2024-01-01',
  batch_size='day',
  lookback=3,
  full_refresh=false
) }}

select * from {{ ref('stg_events') }}

-- Also configure event_time on upstream models that should be auto-filtered.
-- Adapter-specific requirements still apply.
hints: event_time, begin and batch_size are central microbatch configs.
Set event_time on upstream models that should be automatically time-filtered.
items.pitfall: Microbatch is not automatically best for every model; adapter support and a reliable event-time column matter.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  E[Event-time source] --> B1[day -2]
  E --> B2[day -1]
  E --> B3[today]
  B1 --> T[Target]
  B2 --> T
  B3 --> T
  F[failed batch] --> R[retry only failed/bounded batch]
  R --> T

items.title: Choose engine and physical layout from evidence
items.concept: Engine choice and table layout should follow data volume, memory, concurrency, platform constraints, query predicates, writes and observed plans—not brand preference.
items.why: A senior answer explains the decision process and the measurements that would invalidate the first choice.
items.context: Three workloads: 15 GB local Parquet reconciliation; 400 GB read-heavy Fabric Delta mart; 20 TB skewed Spark join pipeline.
items.task: Choose a first engine/layout for each workload, then name the evidence you would measure before scaling or redesigning.
items.starter:
15 GB local reconciliation:
- engine:
- layout:
- measure:

400 GB Fabric mart:
- engine/layout:
- measure:

20 TB distributed join:
- engine/layout:
- measure:
items.solution:
15 GB local reconciliation:
- start with DuckDB for SQL-first analysis or Polars for lazy DataFrame transforms if the machine has comfortable headroom; keep Parquet selective scans. Measure peak memory, bytes read and elapsed time.

400 GB Fabric mart:
- keep Delta/Fabric integration; inspect file count, query predicates and runtime. Consider liquid clustering for read skipping on current Runtime 2.0 guidance; use V-Order/compaction only for the problems they actually solve. Measure files read, query duration and write/maintenance cost.

20 TB distributed join:
- PySpark is justified; inspect the formatted/adaptive plan, shuffle bytes, skew, task durations and join cardinality before adding hardware.

There is no universal GB threshold that makes one engine correct.
hints: Use the smallest sufficient engine, but include operational/platform requirements.
Measure I/O, memory, shuffle, file count and end-to-end latency.
items.pitfall: Do not quote a fixed “Spark starts at X GB” rule as if hardware, row width, compression, joins and concurrency do not matter.

  B -->|no / distributed platform standard| S[PySpark]

  P --> M
  S --> M

items.title: Airflow 3: schedule a DAG from an Asset
items.concept: Airflow Assets model logical data dependencies. In Airflow 3 the concept previously called Dataset is named Asset.
items.why: Data-aware scheduling can express producer/consumer dependencies without hard-coding a clock time between pipelines.
items.context: A consumer DAG should run after the logical silver orders asset is updated successfully.
items.task: Declare an Asset and use it as the consumer DAG schedule.
items.starter:
from airflow.sdk import Asset, DAG
import pendulum

orders_ready = #("s3://lake/silver/orders")

with DAG(
    dag_id='orders_consumer',
    schedule=#,
    start_date=pendulum.datetime(2026, 1, 1, tz='UTC'),
    catchup=False,
):
    ...
items.solution:
from airflow.sdk import Asset, DAG
import pendulum

orders_ready = Asset('s3://lake/silver/orders')

with DAG(
    dag_id='orders_consumer',
    schedule=[orders_ready],
    start_date=pendulum.datetime(2026, 1, 1, tz='UTC'),
    catchup=False,
):
    ...
hints: Asset schedules are lists of Asset objects.
items.pitfall: An Asset URI is a logical identifier, not a glob pattern or a promise that Airflow understands the underlying file contents.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  P[Producer task succeeds] --> A[Asset updated]
  A --> S[Scheduler sees asset event]
  S --> C[Consumer DAG run]

items.title: Airflow 2 → 3: map the breaking concepts
items.concept: Airflow 3 changes both authoring interfaces and deployment architecture: Task SDK/public imports, Assets, API server, independent DAG processor and API v2 are key examples.
items.why: Senior orchestration troubleshooting requires knowing whether a failure is DAG logic, migration compatibility or platform architecture.
items.context: You inherit an Airflow 2.x deployment that uses airflow.decorators, Dataset, the webserver command, REST /api/v1 and SLA callbacks.
items.task: Map each legacy concept to its Airflow 3 direction and list the migration checks you would run before upgrading.
items.starter:
airflow.decorators →
Dataset →
webserver →
REST /api/v1 →
SLA →

PRE-UPGRADE CHECKS:
1.
2.
3.
items.solution:
airflow.decorators / internal authoring imports → airflow.sdk public interface
Dataset → Asset
webserver process → api-server
REST /api/v1 → stable /api/v2
SLA → Deadline Alerts

PRE-UPGRADE CHECKS:
1. Upgrade to a supported recent 2.x baseline (Airflow docs require at least 2.7 before Airflow 3).
2. Back up and clean the metadata DB, then validate DAG serialization.
3. Run the Airflow/Ruff migration checks and review removed/deprecated features before DB migration.
4. Plan the independently running dag-processor and API-server components.
hints: Separate DAG-source migration from deployment-component migration.
A database backup is part of the upgrade plan, not an optional afterthought.
items.pitfall: Do not perform a major Airflow upgrade as a blind pip install while the metadata DB and DAG compatibility are unverified.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  D[Dag file / Task SDK] --> P[Dag processor]
  P --> M[(Metadata DB)]
  S[Scheduler] --> M
  S --> E[Executor / workers]
  E --> T[Task code]
  A[API server] --> M
  T --> X[Data systems]
  X --> AS[Asset update]
  AS --> S

items.title: Structured Streaming: bound state with an event-time watermark
items.concept: Watermarks tell Structured Streaming how late event-time data may arrive so stateful operations can eventually retire old state.
items.why: Without a bounded state strategy, long-running aggregations can retain increasingly large state and become slow or unstable.
items.context: events contains event_time, customer_id and amount. Compute 10-minute revenue windows while allowing events up to 20 minutes late.
items.task: Add a watermark and windowed aggregation.
items.starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

summary = (events
    .#('event_time', '20 minutes')
    .groupBy(#)
    .agg(F.sum('amount').alias('revenue'))
)
items.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

summary = (events
    .withWatermark('event_time', '20 minutes')
    .groupBy(
        F.window('event_time', '10 minutes'),
        F.col('customer_id'),
    )
    .agg(F.sum('amount').alias('revenue'))
)
hints: Use withWatermark before the stateful aggregation.
Window on the same event-time column.
items.pitfall: A watermark is not a business SLA or ingestion-time timeout; it is part of event-time/state management.

flowchart LR

  WM --> SNK[Sink]

  CP --> R[Restart / recovery]
  R --> MB

items.title: Structured Streaming: recover from a durable checkpoint
items.concept: Structured Streaming stores progress and state in the configured checkpoint so a compatible query can continue after a failure/restart.
items.why: A production stream needs a recovery contract, not just a writeStream.start() call.
items.context: Write curated orders to a table and recover offsets/state after a driver restart.
items.task: Configure a durable checkpoint location on the streaming writer.
items.starter:
(curated.writeStream
    .outputMode('append')
    .option(#, #)
    .toTable('silver.orders_stream'))
items.solution:
(curated.writeStream
    .outputMode('append')
    .option('checkpointLocation', 'abfss://checkpoints/orders_stream')
    .toTable('silver.orders_stream'))
hints: checkpointLocation belongs on the streaming writer.
Use storage that survives the driver/process.
items.pitfall: Deleting a checkpoint to make an error disappear changes recovery semantics and can cause reprocessing or lost state.

items.title: Structured Streaming: make foreachBatch writes idempotent
items.concept: foreachBatch gives custom logic per micro-batch and is at-least-once by default; the batch ID can be used to deduplicate output when the sink supports that design.
items.why: A retry can execute a micro-batch write again, so external side effects need their own idempotency contract.
items.context: Each micro-batch is sent to a custom sink that records processed batch IDs.
items.task: Use batch_id to skip an already committed micro-batch.
items.starter:
def write_batch(batch_df, batch_id):
    if #:
        return
    write_to_sink(batch_df)
    #

query = (events.writeStream
    .foreachBatch(write_batch)
    .option('checkpointLocation', 'abfss://checkpoints/custom_sink')
    .start())
items.solution:
def write_batch(batch_df, batch_id):
    if sink_has_batch(batch_id):
        return

    write_to_sink(batch_df)
    mark_batch_committed(batch_id)

query = (events.writeStream
    .foreachBatch(write_batch)
    .option('checkpointLocation', 'abfss://checkpoints/custom_sink')
    .start())

# In a real sink, commit the data + batch marker atomically/transactionally when possible.
hints: Spark passes a unique micro-batch ID to foreachBatch.
The sink must make the dedupe check and commit reliable.
items.pitfall: Checkpointing alone does not magically make arbitrary external foreachBatch side effects exactly-once.

items.title: Structured Streaming: bound a stream-stream join
items.concept: Stateful stream-stream joins need event-time constraints and watermarks so Spark can determine when old join state no longer needs to be retained.
items.why: An unbounded join can accumulate state indefinitely while waiting for a matching event that may never arrive.
items.context: Join orders to payments on order_id. A payment may arrive up to one hour after its order.
items.task: Watermark both streams and add a one-hour event-time range to the join condition.
items.starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

o = orders.#('order_time', '2 hours').alias('o')
p = payments.#('payment_time', '2 hours').alias('p')

joined = o.join(p, #, 'inner')
items.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

o = orders.withWatermark('order_time', '2 hours').alias('o')
p = payments.withWatermark('payment_time', '2 hours').alias('p')

joined = o.join(
    p,
    F.expr(
        "o.order_id = p.order_id AND "
        "p.payment_time >= o.order_time AND "
        "p.payment_time <= o.order_time + INTERVAL 1 HOUR"
    ),
    'inner',
)
hints: Both event-time streams need watermarks for bounded state reasoning.
The join condition needs an event-time range, not only the business key.
items.pitfall: A watermark on one stream plus an equality key alone is not a complete state-cleanup strategy for this join.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  L[Orders stream] --> LW[Watermark orders event time]
  R[Payments stream] --> RW[Watermark payments event time]
  LW --> J[Join key + event-time range]
  RW --> J
  J --> O[Matched output]
  LW -. old unmatched state .-> C[State cleanup]
  RW -. old unmatched state .-> C

items.title: Structured Streaming: know when a checkpoint cannot be reused
items.concept: Checkpoint state encodes assumptions about sources and stateful operators. Some query changes are incompatible with restarting from the same checkpoint.
items.why: A common production incident is deploying a seemingly harmless streaming-code change that conflicts with persisted state.
items.context: A running query groups by customer_id and day. A release changes grouping keys and the state schema but points to the old checkpoint.
items.task: Decide whether to reuse the checkpoint and design a safe migration plan.
items.starter:
REUSE OLD CHECKPOINT?

WHY:

SAFE MIGRATION:
1.
2.
3.
items.solution:
REUSE OLD CHECKPOINT?
- No, not blindly for an incompatible stateful-operator/schema change.

WHY:
- The checkpoint contains persisted progress and state whose schema/partitioning must remain compatible with the restarted query.

SAFE MIGRATION:
1. Read the Spark recovery compatibility rules for the exact change.
2. Deploy a new query/checkpoint when state is incompatible, with an explicit cutover/replay boundary.
3. Reconcile old/new outputs before retiring the previous query.
4. Keep the old checkpoint until rollback risk has passed.
hints: Stateful grouping/aggregate schema changes are particularly sensitive.
Treat a new checkpoint as a data migration/cutover, not a cache clear.
items.pitfall: Never delete production streaming state as the first troubleshooting step just because the restarted query fails.

flowchart LR

  MB --> ET[Event-time transforms]
  ET --> WM[Watermark / bounded state]
  WM --> SNK[Sink]
  MB --> CP[(Checkpoint: offsets + state)]
  CP --> R[Restart / recovery]
  R --> MB

items.title: CDC: transaction log vs polling
items.concept: Log-based change data capture reads database change/replication logs instead of repeatedly querying tables for rows whose timestamps changed.
items.why: CDC can capture inserts, updates and deletes with low latency without requiring a reliable last_updated column or frequent full/table polling.
items.context: An orders database changes continuously and deletes must reach the lakehouse. A polling job currently queries WHERE updated_at > last_watermark every minute.
items.task: Explain when log-based CDC is a better fit, what state the connector must preserve, and one reason polling can miss changes.
items.starter:
POLLING RISKS:
1.
2.

CDC STATE TO PRESERVE:
- 

WHEN CDC FITS:
-
items.solution:
POLLING RISKS:
1. Deletes are invisible unless the source exposes tombstones/soft-delete state.
2. Late or incorrectly maintained timestamps can make updates invisible; aggressive polling also adds source load.

CDC STATE TO PRESERVE:
- The source log/replication position (connector offset) and the schema/history state required to decode changes.

WHEN CDC FITS:
- Frequent operational changes, low-latency replication, delete capture and sources with a usable transaction/replication log.

Polling is still reasonable for small/slow sources or APIs without CDC support.
hints: A CDC connector needs a resumable source position.
items.pitfall: CDC is not automatically exactly-once end to end; downstream consumers still need idempotent keys/write semantics.

    service log(disk)[Transaction log]
    service cdc(server)[CDC connector]
    service stream(server)[Change stream]
    service lake(database)[Lakehouse]
    service offset(disk)[Connector offset]

    db:R --> L:log
    log:R --> L:cdc
    cdc:R --> L:stream
    stream:R --> L:lake
    offset:T --> B:cdc

items.concept: Debezium change events include an operation code plus before/after row state and source metadata. Consumers must preserve the operation semantics when applying changes.

items.pitfall: Do not discard op/source metadata before the sink has correctly applied inserts, updates and deletes.

items.title: CDC: recover after connector downtime
items.concept: CDC recovery depends on a durable source position/offset and the source retaining the transaction or replication history needed from that point onward.
items.why: A connector can restart safely only while its saved position is still usable; long outages and log retention can force a new snapshot/re-bootstrap.
items.context: A connector has been offline for several days. Its saved offset points to source-log history that may already have been purged.
items.task: Write a recovery decision tree before restarting the connector.
items.starter:
1. CHECK SAVED OFFSET:
2. CHECK SOURCE LOG RETENTION:
3. CHECK SCHEMA HISTORY:
4. IF OFFSET IS VALID:
5. IF OFFSET IS NOT VALID:
6. AFTER RECOVERY:
items.solution:
1. CHECK SAVED OFFSET: identify the connector source position and last successfully emitted/committed event.
2. CHECK SOURCE LOG RETENTION: verify the corresponding binlog/WAL/replication history still exists.
3. CHECK SCHEMA HISTORY: ensure the connector can reconstruct table schemas at the resume point.
4. IF OFFSET IS VALID: resume from it and monitor lag until caught up.
5. IF OFFSET IS NOT VALID: use the connector/source-supported re-snapshot or re-bootstrap procedure instead of inventing an offset.
6. AFTER RECOVERY: reconcile source/target keys and counts, then verify delete/update behavior and lag.
hints: The offset is meaningful only if the source can still serve history from that point.
Schema history can matter as much as row-change history.
items.pitfall: Never manually advance an offset only to make a connector start; that can permanently skip source changes.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  DB[(OLTP database)] --> LOG[Transaction / replication log]
  LOG --> DZ[CDC connector]
  DZ --> K[Change-event stream]
  K --> C[Consumer / Spark / sink]
  C --> L[Lakehouse / warehouse]
  DZ --> O[(Offset / source position)]
  O --> DZ

items.title: dbt: enforce a model contract
items.concept: A dbt model contract defines the expected output shape. With contract.enforced: true, declared column names and data types are checked as part of building the model.
items.why: Public marts and shared models should not silently drop or change the type of columns that downstream reports and projects depend on.
items.context: dim_customers is a public table model with customer_id BIGINT, customer_name STRING and created_at TIMESTAMP.
items.task: Write the properties YAML that enables a contract and declares all three columns.
items.starter:
models:
  - name: dim_customers
    config:
      contract:
        enforced: #
    columns:
      - name: customer_id
        data_type: #
      - name: customer_name
        data_type: #
      - name: created_at
        data_type: #
items.solution:
models:
  - name: dim_customers
    config:
      contract:
        enforced: true
    columns:
      - name: customer_id
        data_type: bigint
      - name: customer_name
        data_type: string
      - name: created_at
        data_type: timestamp

# Adapter/platform type names and constraint enforcement differ,
# so use data types understood by your target platform.
hints: Every output column belongs in an enforced model contract.
items.pitfall: Do not assume every declared primary-key/unique/check constraint is physically enforced by every warehouse; platform support varies.

items.title: dbt: model contract vs data test
items.concept: A model contract governs dataset shape such as column names/types; dbt data tests validate data content and business-quality conditions.
items.why: Calling every test a contract hides an important production distinction between interface/schema stability and row-level quality.
items.context: A finance mart must keep revenue as DECIMAL and customer_id present; it must also have no duplicate customer_id values and no negative invoice totals.
items.task: Classify each requirement as model contract, data test, or potentially both/constraint depending on platform.
items.starter:
revenue data type =
customer_id column exists =
customer_id uniqueness =
invoice_total >= 0 =

WHY:
items.solution:
revenue data type = MODEL CONTRACT
customer_id column exists = MODEL CONTRACT
customer_id uniqueness = DATA TEST by default; it may also be a declared/enforced constraint only on platforms that actually support that enforcement
invoice_total >= 0 = DATA TEST by default; a check constraint is platform-dependent

WHY:
- Contract: stable model interface/shape checked while building the model.
- Data test: queryable validation of data content after the model exists.

Use contracts especially for stable/public downstream-facing models rather than every rapidly changing staging model.
hints: Shape versus content is the main distinction.
items.pitfall: Do not say “dbt tests are contracts” without qualification; dbt now has a separate model-contract feature.

items.title: OpenLineage: understand Job, Run and Dataset events
items.concept: OpenLineage models runtime execution with RunEvents and also supports JobEvent and DatasetEvent metadata. RunEvents connect a specific job run to its inputs, outputs and run state.
items.why: Lineage becomes operationally useful when you can distinguish static design metadata from what actually ran and failed.
items.context: An Airflow task transforms raw.orders into silver.orders and fails halfway through a run.
items.task: Map the task name, this execution, raw.orders, silver.orders and FAIL state to the OpenLineage object model.
items.starter:
JOB =
RUN =
INPUT DATASET =
OUTPUT DATASET =
RUN STATE =

WHY THIS MATTERS:
items.solution:
JOB = the logical transformation/task identity
RUN = this specific execution instance with its run ID
INPUT DATASET = raw.orders
OUTPUT DATASET = silver.orders
RUN STATE = FAIL

WHY THIS MATTERS:
A lineage backend can correlate a concrete failed run with affected inputs/outputs instead of only showing a static DAG drawing. START/RUNNING/COMPLETE/FAIL-style runtime events describe the execution lifecycle.
hints: Job is reusable identity; Run is one execution.
items.pitfall: A DAG dependency graph and data lineage overlap, but they are not identical: task ordering alone does not prove which datasets each task actually read or wrote.
items.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Airflow run] --> OL[OpenLineage events]
  S[Spark job] --> OL
  D[dbt model/test] --> OL
  OL --> B[Lineage backend]
  B --> I[Impact analysis]
  B --> T[Troubleshooting]
  B --> R[Backfill / replay scope]

items.title: Use lineage to scope an incident and backfill
items.concept: Cross-tool lineage can connect orchestration runs, Spark jobs, dbt models and datasets so an incident can be scoped by actual upstream/downstream dependencies.
items.why: When a bad source partition is discovered, lineage can reduce the blast radius from “rerun everything” to the affected jobs/datasets and consumers.
items.context: raw.customer_status for 2026-09-03 is wrong. Airflow runs Spark to build silver.customer, then dbt builds dim_customer used by BI.
items.task: Describe how lineage changes your troubleshooting and replay plan.
items.starter:
1. BAD DATASET:
2. DOWNSTREAM IMPACT:
3. FAILED/AFFECTED RUNS:
4. REPLAY SCOPE:
5. VALIDATION:
items.solution:
1. BAD DATASET: identify raw.customer_status and the affected partition/version.
2. DOWNSTREAM IMPACT: follow lineage to Spark silver.customer, dbt dim_customer and registered consumers.
3. FAILED/AFFECTED RUNS: use run metadata to identify executions that consumed the bad input, including successful-but-wrong runs.
4. REPLAY SCOPE: backfill only the affected partition/runs in dependency order with idempotent writes.
5. VALIDATION: reconcile corrected outputs and confirm downstream lineage/consumers now reference corrected data.

Airflow, Spark and dbt all have OpenLineage integration paths, but actual field coverage depends on operators/connectors and configuration.
hints: Successful runs can still have bad data.
Lineage should help bound replay, not replace reconciliation.
items.pitfall: Do not assume automatic lineage is complete for every custom operator/UDF/sink; validate emitted metadata coverage.
items.diagram:
architecture-beta
    service raw(database)[raw.customer_status]
    service spark(server)[Spark transform]
    service silver(database)[silver.customer]
    service dbt(server)[dbt model]
    service dim(database)[dim_customer]
    service bi(server)[BI consumer]
    service lineage(server)[OpenLineage backend]
    service impact(server)[Impact / replay scope]

    raw:R --> L:spark
    spark:R --> L:silver
    silver:R --> L:dbt
    dbt:R --> L:dim
    dim:R --> L:bi
    spark:B --> T:lineage
    dbt:B --> T:lineage
    lineage:R --> L:impact

items.title: Fabric Mirroring vs a hand-built ETL pipeline
items.concept: Fabric Mirroring continuously makes supported operational data available in OneLake; Open Mirroring lets applications/providers land change data that Fabric converts into analytics-ready Delta Parquet.
items.why: Not every source-to-lake movement needs a custom scheduled extract pipeline, but mirroring also does not replace transformation/business-modeling layers.
items.context: An operational SQL source must be available near real time in Fabric for Spark and Power BI. The first requirement is faithful replication, not transformation.
items.task: Choose Mirroring/Open Mirroring or custom ETL and explain what still happens downstream.
items.starter:
INGESTION CHOICE:

WHY:

WHAT MIRRORING HANDLES:
- 

WHAT STILL BELONGS DOWNSTREAM:
-
items.solution:
INGESTION CHOICE:
- Prefer a supported Fabric Mirroring source when available. Use Open Mirroring when a custom provider/application can write the required change files into the OneLake landing zone. Use custom ETL when the source/requirements do not fit mirroring or substantial transformation must happen during ingestion.

WHAT MIRRORING HANDLES:
- continuous replication/change application into OneLake and Delta Parquet representation.

WHAT STILL BELONGS DOWNSTREAM:
- business transformations, quality rules, dimensional/semantic modeling, KPIs and consumer-specific marts.

The mirrored SQL analytics endpoint is for analytics over the replicated copy; it is not the OLTP source.
hints: Mirroring is attractive when the main need is current source data in OneLake.
items.pitfall: Do not describe Mirroring as “no data engineering needed”; quality, modeling, governance and downstream transformations still matter.

architecture-beta

    service mirror(server)[Fabric Mirroring]
    service onelake(disk)[OneLake Delta]
    service sql(database)[SQL endpoint]
    service spark(server)[Spark / Lakehouse]
    service bi(server)[Power BI / consumers]

    source:R --> L:mirror
    mirror:R --> L:onelake
    onelake:R --> L:sql

items.title: Troubleshoot delayed Fabric Mirroring
items.concept: A mirroring delay should be isolated across replication status, source connectivity/configuration, OneLake landing/Delta data and SQL analytics endpoint metadata sync.
items.why: If rows are already in OneLake but absent from the SQL endpoint, restarting the source connector is the wrong first fix.
items.context: Users report that a mirrored table looks stale in SQL. You need to determine whether replication, OneLake data or endpoint metadata is the failing layer.
items.task: Write the diagnostic order and the evidence you would collect.
items.starter:
1. MIRROR STATUS:
2. TABLE LAST COMPLETED / LATENCY:
3. SOURCE:
4. ONELAKE:
5. SQL ENDPOINT:
6. AFTER FIX:
items.solution:
1. MIRROR STATUS: check the mirrored database and per-table replication state/alerts.
2. TABLE LAST COMPLETED / LATENCY: inspect last completed time and, when workspace monitoring is enabled, replication latency evidence.
3. SOURCE: validate source-specific prerequisites, credentials/network/change-feed state and connector limitations.
4. ONELAKE: verify whether the expected Delta data has actually landed; Spark/Lakehouse inspection can separate replication from SQL-endpoint issues.
5. SQL ENDPOINT: if OneLake is current but SQL is stale, investigate metadata synchronization/refresh instead of redoing source replication.
6. AFTER FIX: reconcile business keys/counts and monitor latency until the backlog is cleared.
hints: OneLake current + SQL stale points to a different problem than OneLake stale.
items.pitfall: Do not repeatedly stop/start mirroring before preserving status, latency and source evidence; that can make root-cause analysis harder.
items.diagram:
architecture-beta
    service source(database)[Source changes]
    service replication(server)[Replication status]
    service onelake(disk)[OneLake Delta]
    service sql(database)[SQL metadata]
    service consumer(server)[Consumer query]

    source:R --> L:replication
    replication:R --> L:onelake
    onelake:R --> L:sql
    sql:R --> L:consumer

items.title: Build every size × brand combination
items.concept: CROSS JOIN returns the Cartesian product: every row from the first input paired with every row from the second.
items.context: Tables: dbo.sizes(size_code) with XS, M, L, XL; dbo.brands(brand_name) with Nike, Asphalte, Abercrombie, Lewis.
items.task: Return every possible size and brand combination. Before revealing the solution, predict the output row count.
items.starter:
SELECT
    -- columns
FROM dbo.sizes AS s
-- join dbo.brands
items.solution:
SELECT
    s.size_code,
    b.brand_name
FROM dbo.sizes AS s
CROSS JOIN dbo.brands AS b;
items.solutionExplanation: There is no join predicate because a cross join intentionally creates all combinations. With 4 sizes and 4 brands, the result has 16 rows.
hints: A CROSS JOIN has no ON clause.
items.pitfall: Adding an ON condition changes the problem into a conditional join rather than a Cartesian product.

items.title: Generate quarter-hour time slots
items.concept: A small Cartesian product is useful for generating complete dimensional combinations.
items.context: Tables: dbo.hours(hour_value) contains 08–12; dbo.quarters(minute_value) contains 00, 15, 30, 45.
items.task: Generate every hour/minute pair and sort chronologically.
items.starter:
SELECT
    h.hour_value,
    q.minute_value
FROM dbo.hours AS h
-- complete the join
-- order the result
items.solution:
SELECT
    h.hour_value,
    q.minute_value
FROM dbo.hours AS h
CROSS JOIN dbo.quarters AS q
ORDER BY h.hour_value, q.minute_value;
items.solutionExplanation: The two tiny dimensions are independent, so CROSS JOIN creates the full grid. ORDER BY makes the generated combinations readable as time slots.
hints: Join every hour to every quarter.
Sort by hour first, then minute.
items.pitfall: Do not use INNER JOIN unless you invent a key; that obscures the intent.

items.title: Build a complete retail reporting grid
items.concept: Cross joins can generate a scaffold containing combinations that do not yet exist in fact data.
items.context: Dimensions: dbo.stores(store_id), dbo.markets(market_id), dbo.months(month_id), dbo.weekdays(weekday_id), dbo.quarters(quarter_id).
items.task: Create every store × market × month × weekday × quarter combination.
items.starter:
SELECT
    s.store_id, m.market_id, mo.month_id, w.weekday_id, q.quarter_id
FROM dbo.stores AS s
-- add the remaining dimensions
items.solution:
SELECT
    s.store_id,
    m.market_id,
    mo.month_id,
    w.weekday_id,
    q.quarter_id
FROM dbo.stores AS s
CROSS JOIN dbo.markets AS m
CROSS JOIN dbo.months AS mo
CROSS JOIN dbo.weekdays AS w
CROSS JOIN dbo.quarters AS q;
items.solutionExplanation: Each additional CROSS JOIN multiplies the current row count by the size of the next dimension. This pattern is useful for gap detection, but the cardinality must be estimated first.
hints: There is still no ON predicate.
Estimate the row count before running this in production.
items.pitfall: Cartesian products can explode in size very quickly; use them intentionally and with small dimensions.

items.why: This pattern appears in data transformation, reconciliation, quality checks, reporting queries, and data-engineering interviews.
items.title: Match customers to detailed orders
items.concept: INNER JOIN keeps only rows that satisfy the join predicate on both sides.
items.context: dbo.customers(customer_id, customer_name); dbo.order_detail(order_id, customer_id, product_id, quantity).
items.task: Return customer_id, customer_name, order_id, product_id, and quantity for customers that have matching order details.
items.starter:
SELECT
    -- requested columns
FROM dbo.customers AS c
INNER JOIN dbo.order_detail AS od
    ON -- matching key
items.solution:
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.customer_name,
    od.order_id,
    od.product_id,
    od.quantity
FROM dbo.customers AS c
INNER JOIN dbo.order_detail AS od
    ON c.customer_id = od.customer_id;
items.solutionExplanation: The equality predicate connects the customer business key to the foreign key in the order details. Customers without matching details disappear by design.
hints: Qualify customer_id because it exists in both tables.
items.pitfall: Joining on unrelated columns can produce plausible-looking but incorrect data.

items.title: Enrich order rows with product data
items.concept: Joins are often chained: first establish the transaction grain, then enrich it with dimensions.
items.context: dbo.customer_orders already contains product_id; dbo.products(product_id, product_name, unit_price).
items.task: Return all matched order rows enriched with the product name and unit price.
items.starter:
SELECT
    co.*,
    -- product columns
FROM dbo.customer_orders AS co
-- join products
items.solution:
SELECT
    co.*,
    p.product_name,
    p.unit_price
FROM dbo.customer_orders AS co
INNER JOIN dbo.products AS p
    ON co.product_id = p.product_id;
items.solutionExplanation: The product_id is the relationship key. INNER JOIN assumes rows without a known product should not appear in this result.
hints: Use table aliases to make the key origin obvious.
items.pitfall: If unknown products must remain visible for data-quality analysis, LEFT JOIN would be the better choice.

items.title: Map each sale to its retail universe
items.concept: A normalized model may require several joins to move from a fact table to a higher-level business category.
items.context: dbo.sales(product_id,...); dbo.product_category(product_id, category_id); dbo.category_universe(category_id, universe_id).
items.task: Return sales with the category_id and universe_id by chaining two inner joins.
items.starter:
SELECT
    s.*,
    pc.category_id,
    cu.universe_id
FROM dbo.sales AS s
-- join product_category
-- join category_universe
items.solution:
SELECT
    s.*,
    pc.category_id,
    cu.universe_id
FROM dbo.sales AS s
INNER JOIN dbo.product_category AS pc
    ON s.product_id = pc.product_id
INNER JOIN dbo.category_universe AS cu
    ON pc.category_id = cu.category_id;
items.solutionExplanation: The first join resolves product → category; the second resolves category → universe. Each predicate follows a declared relationship rather than guessing from names.
hints: Then use category_id to reach the universe.
items.pitfall: Do not join sales directly to category_universe unless a legitimate key exists between them.

FROM dbo.actual_sales AS a

    a.amount,
    t.target_amount
FROM dbo.actual_sales AS a
INNER JOIN dbo.product_targets AS t

items.title: Understand a cross join simulated with an inner join
items.concept: If every row on both sides has the same artificial key, an inner join on that key creates a Cartesian product.
items.context: dbo.beverages(id, beverage) and dbo.food_items(id, food) both have id = 1 for every row.
items.task: Write the inner join that produces every beverage × food pair. Then identify why CROSS JOIN would express the intention more clearly.
items.starter:
SELECT b.beverage, f.food
FROM dbo.beverages AS b
INNER JOIN dbo.food_items AS f
    ON -- constant key match
items.solution:
SELECT
    b.beverage,
    f.food
FROM dbo.beverages AS b
INNER JOIN dbo.food_items AS f
    ON b.id = f.id;
items.solutionExplanation: Because every id is 1, every beverage matches every food. It works, but CROSS JOIN is clearer because it states that the Cartesian product is intentional.
hints: Every row has the same id.
Think about how many rows match each left row.
items.pitfall: Do not use this artificial-key trick in real code when CROSS JOIN expresses the intent directly.

items.title: Keep customers even when they have no orders
items.concept: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills unmatched right-side columns with NULL.
items.context: dbo.customers(customer_id, customer_name); dbo.order_detail(order_id, customer_id, product_id, quantity).
items.task: Return all customers and any matching order detail. Customers without orders must remain in the result.
items.starter:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name, od.order_id, od.product_id, od.quantity
FROM dbo.customers AS c
-- complete the left join
items.solution:
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.customer_name,
    od.order_id,
    od.product_id,
    od.quantity
FROM dbo.customers AS c
LEFT JOIN dbo.order_detail AS od
    ON c.customer_id = od.customer_id;
items.solutionExplanation: The preserved side is dbo.customers because it appears before LEFT JOIN. Missing orders show as NULL rather than removing the customer.
hints: Put the dataset you must preserve on the left.
items.pitfall: Reversing the table order changes which records are guaranteed to survive.

items.title: Find sales with no mapped universe
items.concept: LEFT JOIN plus an IS NULL filter is an anti-join pattern for detecting unmatched keys.
items.context: dbo.sales(product_id,...); dbo.product_category(product_id, category_id); dbo.category_universe(category_id, universe_id).
items.task: Find sales that cannot be mapped to a universe. Preserve sales through both joins, then keep rows where universe_id is NULL.
items.starter:
SELECT s.*, pc.category_id, cu.universe_id
FROM dbo.sales AS s
-- left join mappings
WHERE -- missing universe
items.solution:
SELECT
    s.*,
    pc.category_id,
    cu.universe_id
FROM dbo.sales AS s
LEFT JOIN dbo.product_category AS pc
    ON s.product_id = pc.product_id
LEFT JOIN dbo.category_universe AS cu
    ON pc.category_id = cu.category_id
WHERE cu.universe_id IS NULL;
items.solutionExplanation: Both enrichment steps are left joins so unmapped sales survive. The final IS NULL test isolates the failures.
hints: The missing value appears on the right-most dimension.
Filter with IS NULL, not = NULL.
items.pitfall: `= NULL` never behaves like an ordinary equality comparison; use IS NULL.

items.title: Keep the left join while filtering the right table
items.concept: A predicate in ON controls matching; the same predicate in WHERE can remove NULL-extended rows after the join.
items.context: dbo.customers; dbo.orders(customer_id, order_date, status).
items.task: Return every customer and only their 2026 completed orders. Customers with no matching completed 2026 order must still appear.
items.starter:
SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id, o.order_date
FROM dbo.customers AS c
LEFT JOIN dbo.orders AS o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
   AND -- put right-side filters here
items.solution:
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    o.order_id,
    o.order_date
FROM dbo.customers AS c
LEFT JOIN dbo.orders AS o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
   AND o.status = 'COMPLETED'
   AND o.order_date >= '20260101'

items.title: Preserve store products and catalog products
items.concept: FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both inputs.
items.context: dbo.store_products(product_id, store_id); dbo.products(product_id, product_name).
items.task: Return every store-product mapping and every catalog product, including products missing on either side.
items.starter:
SELECT sp.store_id, COALESCE(sp.product_id, p.product_id) AS product_id, p.product_name
FROM dbo.store_products AS sp
-- full join products
items.solution:
SELECT
    sp.store_id,
    COALESCE(sp.product_id, p.product_id) AS product_id,
    p.product_name
FROM dbo.store_products AS sp
FULL OUTER JOIN dbo.products AS p
    ON sp.product_id = p.product_id;
items.solutionExplanation: Matched products appear once; unmatched store mappings and unmatched catalog products are both preserved. COALESCE provides whichever product_id exists.
hints: The key can be NULL on either side after the join.
items.pitfall: SELECTing only one side’s key can hide the identifier for rows that exist only on the other side.

items.title: Reconcile source and target customer IDs
items.concept: FULL OUTER JOIN is useful for reconciliation: matched, source-only, and target-only records can be classified in one result.
items.context: dbo.source_customers(customer_id); dbo.target_customers(customer_id).
items.task: Return customer_id and a status of MATCHED, SOURCE_ONLY, or TARGET_ONLY.
items.starter:
SELECT
    COALESCE(s.customer_id, t.customer_id) AS customer_id,
    CASE
        -- classify the row
    END AS reconciliation_status
FROM dbo.source_customers AS s
FULL OUTER JOIN dbo.target_customers AS t
    ON s.customer_id = t.customer_id;
items.solution:
SELECT
    COALESCE(s.customer_id, t.customer_id) AS customer_id,
    CASE
        WHEN s.customer_id IS NULL THEN 'TARGET_ONLY'
        WHEN t.customer_id IS NULL THEN 'SOURCE_ONLY'
        ELSE 'MATCHED'
    END AS reconciliation_status
FROM dbo.source_customers AS s
FULL OUTER JOIN dbo.target_customers AS t
    ON s.customer_id = t.customer_id;
items.solutionExplanation: The NULL pattern tells you which side was missing. This is a common migration and pipeline validation query.
items.pitfall: Do not filter out NULLs before classifying them; those NULLs are the signal you need.

items.title: Resolve employee → manager names
items.concept: A self join uses two aliases for the same table so rows can play different roles.
items.context: dbo.employees(employee_id, employee_name, manager_id).
items.task: Return each employee with their manager name. Keep top-level employees who have no manager.
items.starter:
SELECT e.employee_name, m.employee_name AS manager_name
FROM dbo.employees AS e
-- join dbo.employees again as m
items.solution:
SELECT
    e.employee_name,
    m.employee_name AS manager_name
FROM dbo.employees AS e
LEFT JOIN dbo.employees AS m
    ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;
items.solutionExplanation: Alias e represents the employee row; alias m represents the manager row. LEFT JOIN keeps executives whose manager_id is NULL.
hints: Use the same table twice with different aliases.
items.pitfall: Without aliases, the column references are ambiguous and the relationship is hard to read.

items.title: Find customers ordering on consecutive days
items.concept: Self joins can compare different rows belonging to the same entity.
items.context: dbo.sales_orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date).
items.task: Return pairs of different orders for the same customer where the second order occurs exactly one day after the first.
items.starter:
SELECT a.customer_id, a.order_id AS first_order, b.order_id AS second_order
FROM dbo.sales_orders AS a
INNER JOIN dbo.sales_orders AS b
    ON -- same customer
   AND -- next day relationship
items.solution:
SELECT
    a.customer_id,
    a.order_id AS first_order,
    a.order_date AS first_order_date,
    b.order_id AS second_order,
    b.order_date AS second_order_date
FROM dbo.sales_orders AS a
INNER JOIN dbo.sales_orders AS b
    ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id
   AND b.order_date = DATEADD(day, 1, a.order_date);
items.solutionExplanation: The date relationship itself guarantees the rows are different, so a separate order_id inequality is usually unnecessary. DATEADD is idiomatic T-SQL.
hints: Join rows for the same customer.
items.pitfall: Joining only on customer_id creates every order pair for that customer and can become quadratic.

items.title: Find Benjamin’s meeting partners
items.concept: A many-participant event table can be self-joined on event ID to build participant pairs.
items.context: dbo.meeting_participants(meeting_id, person_name, duration_minutes).
items.task: Return Benjamin’s meetings paired with every other participant in the same meeting.
items.starter:
SELECT a.meeting_id, b.person_name AS colleague, a.duration_minutes
FROM dbo.meeting_participants AS a
INNER JOIN dbo.meeting_participants AS b
    ON -- same meeting
WHERE -- Benjamin on left, someone else on right
items.solution:
SELECT
    a.meeting_id,
    b.person_name AS colleague,
    a.duration_minutes
FROM dbo.meeting_participants AS a
INNER JOIN dbo.meeting_participants AS b
    ON a.meeting_id = b.meeting_id
WHERE a.person_name = 'Benjamin'
  AND b.person_name <> 'Benjamin';
items.solutionExplanation: The self join expands each Benjamin event row to the other participants in that event. A later GROUP BY can summarize time by colleague.
hints: Filter the left alias to Benjamin.
Exclude Benjamin from the right alias.
items.pitfall: Forgetting the right-side exclusion pairs Benjamin with himself.

items.title: Average property price by neighborhood
items.concept: GROUP BY changes the grain of the result to one row per grouping key.
items.context: dbo.property_sales(neighborhood, price).

items.title: Filter aggregated cities with HAVING
items.concept: WHERE filters input rows before aggregation; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
items.context: dbo.property_sales(city, sale_value).
items.task: Return cities with more than 10 sales and average sale value below 250000.
items.starter:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS sale_count, AVG(sale_value) AS avg_sale_value
FROM dbo.property_sales
GROUP BY city
-- filter the groups
items.solution:
SELECT
    city,
    COUNT(*) AS sale_count,
    AVG(sale_value) AS avg_sale_value
FROM dbo.property_sales
GROUP BY city
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10
   AND AVG(sale_value) < 250000;
items.solutionExplanation: The conditions depend on COUNT and AVG, which do not exist until after grouping. HAVING is therefore the correct filter stage.
hints: You are filtering groups, not raw rows.
items.pitfall: Trying to use aggregate aliases in WHERE is logically too early.

items.title: Customers above the global average transaction value
items.concept: A grouped aggregate can be compared with a scalar aggregate computed by a subquery.
items.context: dbo.sales(customer_id, amount).
items.task: Return customers whose average transaction amount is greater than the average amount across all transactions.
items.solution:
SELECT
    customer_id,
    AVG(amount) AS customer_avg
FROM dbo.sales
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING AVG(amount) > (
    SELECT AVG(amount)
    FROM dbo.sales
);
items.solutionExplanation: The inner query returns one scalar global benchmark. HAVING compares each customer-level aggregate to that benchmark.
hints: The subquery should return exactly one value.
The outer query groups by customer_id.
items.pitfall: Grouping the inner query would return multiple values and break the scalar comparison.

items.title: Rewrite the global-average filter with a CTE
items.concept: A CTE can give a named intermediate result to a benchmark or complex aggregation.
items.context: dbo.sales(customer_id, amount).
items.task: Compute the global average in a CTE, then return customers whose average transaction amount is above it.
items.starter:
WITH global_avg AS (
    -- one-row benchmark
)
SELECT customer_id, AVG(amount) AS customer_avg
FROM dbo.sales
-- bring benchmark into scope
GROUP BY customer_id, -- benchmark column
HAVING -- compare averages
items.solution:
WITH global_avg AS (
    SELECT AVG(amount) AS avg_amount
    FROM dbo.sales
)
SELECT
    s.customer_id,
    AVG(s.amount) AS customer_avg
FROM dbo.sales AS s
CROSS JOIN global_avg AS g
GROUP BY s.customer_id, g.avg_amount
HAVING AVG(s.amount) > g.avg_amount;
items.solutionExplanation: The one-row CTE is cross joined so its scalar benchmark is available to the grouped query. Because g.avg_amount appears as a non-aggregated selected/reference value at group scope, it is included in GROUP BY.
hints: A one-row CTE can be CROSS JOINed safely.
items.pitfall: A CTE does not automatically expose its columns; it must be referenced in FROM/JOIN.

items.title: Average meeting duration by colleague
items.concept: A CTE can first construct the correct row grain, then a GROUP BY can summarize it.
items.context: dbo.meeting_participants(meeting_id, person_name, duration_minutes).
items.task: Using a self-join CTE, calculate Benjamin’s average meeting duration with each colleague.
items.solution:
WITH benjamin_meetings AS (
    SELECT
        a.meeting_id,
        b.person_name AS colleague,
        a.duration_minutes
    FROM dbo.meeting_participants AS a
    INNER JOIN dbo.meeting_participants AS b
        ON a.meeting_id = b.meeting_id
    WHERE a.person_name = 'Benjamin'
      AND b.person_name <> 'Benjamin'
)
SELECT
    colleague,
    AVG(duration_minutes) AS avg_meeting_duration
FROM benjamin_meetings
GROUP BY colleague;
items.solutionExplanation: The CTE creates one Benjamin-colleague row per shared meeting; the outer query changes the grain to one row per colleague.
hints: Aggregate only after the colleague rows exist.
items.pitfall: Aggregating before forming participant pairs loses the relationship you need.

items.title: Apply salary raises by department
items.concept: Searched CASE evaluates conditions in order and returns the result for the first matching branch.
items.context: dbo.employees(employee_name, department, wage). SALES +10%, HR +5%, IT +3%, everyone else unchanged.
items.task: Return employee_name, department, wage, and wage_after_raise.
items.starter:
SELECT employee_name, department, wage,
       CASE
           -- department rules
           ELSE wage
       END AS wage_after_raise
FROM dbo.employees;
items.solution:
SELECT
    employee_name,
    department,
    wage,
    CASE
        WHEN department = 'SALES' THEN wage * 1.10
        WHEN department = 'HR' THEN wage * 1.05
        WHEN department = 'IT' THEN wage * 1.03
        ELSE wage
    END AS wage_after_raise
FROM dbo.employees;
items.solutionExplanation: CASE creates a derived value per row. ELSE preserves the original wage for departments without a special rule.
hints: Each WHEN returns a numeric expression.
items.pitfall: Forgetting ELSE returns NULL for unmatched departments.

items.title: Calculate discounted revenue with a CTE
items.concept: A CTE can make row-level business rules explicit before aggregation.
items.context: dbo.sales(discount_code, quantity, price_per_unit). DISCOUNT10 = 10% off; DISCOUNT20 = 20% off.
items.task: In a CTE, compute revenue_after_discount for every row, then return total revenue by discount_code.
items.starter:
WITH priced AS (
    SELECT discount_code,
           CASE
               -- discount rules
           END AS revenue_after_discount
    FROM dbo.sales
)
SELECT discount_code, SUM(revenue_after_discount) AS total_revenue
FROM priced
GROUP BY discount_code;
items.solution:
WITH priced AS (
    SELECT
        discount_code,
        CASE
            WHEN discount_code = 'DISCOUNT10' THEN quantity * price_per_unit * 0.90
            WHEN discount_code = 'DISCOUNT20' THEN quantity * price_per_unit * 0.80
            ELSE quantity * price_per_unit
        END AS revenue_after_discount
    FROM dbo.sales
)
SELECT
    discount_code,
    SUM(revenue_after_discount) AS total_revenue
FROM priced
GROUP BY discount_code;
items.solutionExplanation: The CTE separates row-level pricing rules from the group-level SUM, which makes the logic easier to debug.
hints: SUM belongs in the outer query.
items.pitfall: Multiplying by 0.10 would keep only 10% of revenue; a 10% discount means multiply by 0.90.

items.title: Bucket salaries then aggregate
items.concept: CASE can create a categorical dimension that is then used in a GROUP BY.
items.context: dbo.employees(department, wage). Low ≤ 50000; Medium < 90000; otherwise High.
items.task: Create salary_band in a CTE, then return department, salary_band, employee_count, and average_wage.
items.starter:
WITH banded AS (
    SELECT department, wage,
           CASE
               -- bands
           END AS salary_band
    FROM dbo.employees
)
SELECT department, salary_band,
       -- count and average
FROM banded
GROUP BY department, salary_band;
items.solution:
WITH banded AS (
    SELECT
        department,
        wage,
        CASE
            WHEN wage <= 50000 THEN 'Low'
            WHEN wage < 90000 THEN 'Medium'
            ELSE 'High'
        END AS salary_band
    FROM dbo.employees
)
SELECT
    department,
    salary_band,
    COUNT(*) AS employee_count,
    AVG(wage) AS average_wage
FROM banded
GROUP BY department, salary_band;
items.solutionExplanation: The CTE materializes the business classification logically; the outer query aggregates at department + band grain.
hints: Order the thresholds from low to high.
COUNT(*) gives the number of employees in each group.
items.pitfall: Overlapping or incorrectly ordered WHEN conditions can classify rows into the wrong bucket.

WITH banded AS (
    SELECT department, wage,
           CASE
               -- bands
           END AS salary_band
    FROM dbo.employees
)
SELECT department, salary_band,
       -- count and average
FROM banded
GROUP BY department, salary_band;
original.solution:
WITH banded AS (
    SELECT
        department,
        wage,
        CASE
            WHEN wage <= 50000 THEN 'Low'
            WHEN wage < 90000 THEN 'Medium'
            ELSE 'High'
        END AS salary_band
    FROM dbo.employees
)
SELECT
    department,
    salary_band,
    COUNT(*) AS employee_count,
    AVG(wage) AS average_wage
FROM banded
GROUP BY department, salary_band;
original.solutionExplanation: The CTE materializes the business classification logically; the outer query aggregates at department + band grain.
hints: Order the thresholds from low to high.
COUNT(*) gives the number of employees in each group.
original.pitfall: Overlapping or incorrectly ordered WHEN conditions can classify rows into the wrong bucket.

items.title: Count home and away wins conditionally
items.concept: COUNT(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END) counts only rows where CASE returns a non-NULL value.
items.context: dbo.matches(division, home_team, away_team, home_goals, away_goals). Count Lille wins in division L1.
items.task: Return the number of Lille home wins and away wins for L1 in one query.
items.starter:
SELECT
    COUNT(CASE WHEN -- home win THEN 1 END) AS home_wins,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN -- away win THEN 1 END) AS away_wins
FROM dbo.matches
WHERE division = 'L1';
items.solution:
SELECT
    COUNT(CASE
        WHEN home_team = 'Lille' AND home_goals > away_goals THEN 1
    END) AS home_wins,
    COUNT(CASE
        WHEN away_team = 'Lille' AND away_goals > home_goals THEN 1
    END) AS away_wins
FROM dbo.matches
WHERE division = 'L1';
items.solutionExplanation: COUNT ignores NULL. The CASE returns 1 only for a qualifying win, so each aggregate counts its own condition.
hints: Home win: Lille is home and home_goals > away_goals.
Filter the division separately in WHERE.
items.pitfall: `ELSE 0` inside COUNT would count zeros too, because zero is non-NULL. Use no ELSE, or use SUM with ELSE 0.

items.title: Combine two separate summaries with UNION ALL
items.concept: GROUPING SETS can replace patterns that otherwise require multiple grouped queries combined with UNION ALL.
items.context: dbo.reimbursements(contract_type, act_type, amount_reimbursed).
items.task: Return totals by contract_type and totals by act_type as a single two-column result named typology, total_reimbursed. Use UNION ALL.
items.starter:
SELECT contract_type AS typology, SUM(amount_reimbursed) AS total_reimbursed
FROM dbo.reimbursements
GROUP BY contract_type

UNION ALL

-- second aggregation
items.solution:
SELECT
    contract_type AS typology,
    SUM(amount_reimbursed) AS total_reimbursed
FROM dbo.reimbursements
GROUP BY contract_type

UNION ALL

SELECT
    act_type AS typology,
    SUM(amount_reimbursed) AS total_reimbursed
FROM dbo.reimbursements
GROUP BY act_type;
items.solutionExplanation: Two independent groupings are computed separately and stacked. The next challenge replaces this with GROUPING SETS in one grouped query.
hints: Both SELECTs must return compatible columns.
Use UNION ALL so rows are not unnecessarily deduplicated.
items.pitfall: UNION performs duplicate elimination; UNION ALL is usually the intended operation for combining grouping results.

items.title: Replace two GROUP BY queries with GROUPING SETS
items.concept: GROUPING SETS computes explicitly requested aggregation grains in one GROUP BY.
items.context: dbo.reimbursements(contract_type, act_type, amount_reimbursed).
items.task: Return totals by contract_type and totals by act_type using GROUPING SETS.
items.solution:
SELECT
    contract_type,
    act_type,
    SUM(amount_reimbursed) AS total_reimbursed
FROM dbo.reimbursements
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (
    (contract_type),
    (act_type)
);
items.solutionExplanation: The engine computes two grains: one where contract_type is grouped and one where act_type is grouped. The other grouping column is NULL in each subtotal row.
hints: Each grouping set is written in parentheses.
You need one set for each desired grain.
items.pitfall: `(contract_type, act_type)` is one combined grain; `(contract_type), (act_type)` are two separate grains.

items.title: Region/year detail plus yearly totals
items.concept: Grouping sets can produce detail and subtotal levels together.
items.context: dbo.population(year_value, region, population).
items.task: Return population by year + region and also total population by year.
items.solution:
SELECT
    year_value,
    region,
    SUM(population) AS population
FROM dbo.population
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (
    (year_value, region),
    (year_value)
);
items.solutionExplanation: The first grouping set gives regional detail; the second collapses region to produce one subtotal per year.
hints: Write the most detailed grain first.

items.title: Label subtotal rows with GROUPING()
items.concept: GROUPING(column) distinguishes subtotal NULL placeholders from real NULL values in source data.
items.context: dbo.population(year_value, region, population).
items.task: Use GROUPING SETS for region/year detail and yearly totals. Return region_label = ALL REGIONS for subtotal rows.
items.starter:
SELECT year_value,
       CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'ALL REGIONS' ELSE region END AS region_label,
       SUM(population) AS population
FROM dbo.population
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((year_value, region), (year_value));
items.solution:
SELECT
    year_value,
    CASE
        WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'ALL REGIONS'
        ELSE region
    END AS region_label,
    SUM(population) AS population
FROM dbo.population

items.title: Product share of store sales with grouping sets
items.concept: Grouping sets can compute detail and total rows in one aggregation, then those rows can be joined or conditionally aggregated to calculate shares.
items.context: dbo.sales(store_id, product_name, amount). Compute Red Bull sales divided by total store sales.
items.task: Use GROUPING SETS to compute product-level and store-level totals, then return Red Bull share for each store.
items.starter:
WITH totals AS (
    SELECT store_id, product_name, SUM(amount) AS amount
    FROM dbo.sales
    GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (
        -- product detail and store total
    )
)
-- join/aggregate totals to calculate Red Bull share
items.solution:
WITH totals AS (
    SELECT
        store_id,
        product_name,
        SUM(amount) AS amount
    FROM dbo.sales
    GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (
        (store_id, product_name),
        (store_id)
    )
), store_rollup AS (
    SELECT
        store_id,
        MAX(CASE WHEN product_name = 'Red Bull' THEN amount END) AS red_bull_sales,
        MAX(CASE WHEN product_name IS NULL THEN amount END) AS store_sales
    FROM totals
    GROUP BY store_id
)
SELECT
    store_id,
    red_bull_sales,
    store_sales,
    red_bull_sales * 1.0 / NULLIF(store_sales, 0) AS red_bull_share
FROM store_rollup;
items.solutionExplanation: The first CTE emits both product rows and store-total rows. The second CTE pivots the two required values into one row per store before dividing.
hints: Your grouping sets are (store_id, product_name) and (store_id).
The store subtotal has product_name = NULL.
Use NULLIF to guard division by zero.
items.pitfall: Treat subtotal NULLs carefully if product_name can genuinely be NULL in source data; GROUPING(product_name) is safer in that case.

items.title: Repeat a grand total on every row with OVER()
items.concept: An aggregate used with OVER() becomes a window aggregate: rows are retained while the aggregate is calculated across the window.
items.context: dbo.sensor_daily(date_value, visitors_count).
items.task: Return every row and add total_visitors containing the grand total visitors across the full table.
items.solution:
SELECT
    *,
    SUM(visitors_count) OVER () AS total_visitors
FROM dbo.sensor_daily;
items.solutionExplanation: Without GROUP BY, the detail rows remain. OVER() tells SQL Server to calculate the SUM over the complete result window and repeat it on each row.
items.pitfall: `SUM(visitors_count)` without OVER and without GROUP BY collapses the result to a single aggregate row.

items.title: Running total by date
items.concept: ORDER BY inside OVER defines the logical sequence for a running calculation.
items.context: dbo.sensor_daily(date_value, visitors_count), one row per date.
items.task: Add running_visitors: cumulative visitors from the first date through the current row.
items.solution:
SELECT
    date_value,
    visitors_count,
    SUM(visitors_count) OVER (
        ORDER BY date_value
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_visitors
FROM dbo.sensor_daily;
items.solutionExplanation: The explicit ROWS frame makes the running-total behavior deterministic by row position from the beginning through the current row.
hints: Use UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to start at the first row.
items.pitfall: Relying on an implicit frame can be confusing when ORDER BY values contain ties; explicit ROWS is clearer.

items.title: Centered five-row moving average
items.concept: A ROWS frame can include rows before and after the current row.
items.context: dbo.daily_sales(date_value, daily_sales).
items.task: Compute a five-row moving average: two rows before, current row, and two rows after.
items.solution:
SELECT
    date_value,
    daily_sales,
    AVG(daily_sales * 1.0) OVER (
        ORDER BY date_value
        ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 2 FOLLOWING
    ) AS moving_average
FROM dbo.daily_sales;
items.solutionExplanation: The frame contains at most five physical rows centered on the current row. At the edges, SQL uses only the rows that exist.
items.pitfall: ROWS counts physical rows, not “days.” Missing dates change the business meaning unless the data is calendar-complete.

items.title: Trailing seven-row moving average
items.concept: A trailing frame includes a fixed number of preceding rows plus the current row.
items.context: dbo.sensor_daily(date_value, visitors_count), one row per calendar day.
items.task: Compute the average visitors across the current day and previous six rows.
items.solution:
SELECT
    *,
    AVG(visitors_count * 1.0) OVER (
        ORDER BY date_value
        ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS seven_day_avg
FROM dbo.sensor_daily;
items.solutionExplanation: Six preceding rows plus the current row gives a maximum frame size of seven. This corresponds to seven days only when the table has exactly one row per day.
hints: Use CURRENT ROW as the end boundary.
items.pitfall: A seven-row window is not automatically a seven-day window if dates are missing or duplicated.

items.why: This pattern appears in data transformation, reconciliation, quality checks, reporting queries, and data-engineering interviews.
items.title: Verify a moving average with SUM / COUNT
items.concept: AVG over a frame can be validated by calculating SUM and COUNT over the exact same frame.
items.context: dbo.sensor_daily(date_value, visitors_count).
items.task: Return trailing-seven-row SUM, COUNT, manual_average = SUM/COUNT, and AVG using identical frames.
items.starter:
SELECT *,
       -- SUM window
       -- COUNT window
       -- manual division
       -- AVG window
FROM dbo.sensor_daily;
items.solution:
WITH w AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        SUM(visitors_count) OVER (
            ORDER BY date_value
            ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
        ) AS window_sum,
        COUNT(*) OVER (
            ORDER BY date_value
            ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
        ) AS window_count,
        AVG(visitors_count * 1.0) OVER (
            ORDER BY date_value
            ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
        ) AS window_avg
    FROM dbo.sensor_daily
)
SELECT
    *,
    window_sum * 1.0 / NULLIF(window_count, 0) AS manual_avg
FROM w;
items.solutionExplanation: All three functions use the same frame. The outer SELECT makes the manual calculation readable and avoids repeating the window expressions.
hints: Every window must use the same ORDER BY and frame.
Use a CTE so aliases can be reused.
items.pitfall: SQL Server generally does not let you reference a SELECT-list alias in another expression in the same SELECT list.

items.title: Flag the highest-paid employee in each department
items.concept: A group benchmark from a window function can be compared to the current row in an outer query.
items.context: dbo.employees(employee_name, department, wage).
items.task: Add department_max_wage and is_top_earner (1/0).
items.starter:
WITH x AS (
    SELECT *,
           MAX(wage) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS department_max_wage
    FROM dbo.employees
)
SELECT *,
       CASE WHEN -- compare wage to max -- END AS is_top_earner
FROM x;
items.solution:
WITH x AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        MAX(wage) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS department_max_wage
    FROM dbo.employees
)
SELECT
    *,
    CASE WHEN wage = department_max_wage THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_top_earner
FROM x;
items.solutionExplanation: The CTE calculates the partition benchmark first; the outer query can then reference the alias cleanly.
hints: Compare current wage to the window result in an outer query.
items.pitfall: If two employees tie for maximum wage, both should be flagged; ROW_NUMBER would arbitrarily choose one unless you add a tie-breaker.

items.title: Second distinct highest wage per department
items.concept: Ranking functions are usually clearer than repeated max-filter-max logic for nth-highest problems.
items.context: dbo.employees(employee_name, department, wage).
items.task: Return employees whose wage is the second distinct highest wage in their department.
items.starter:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (
               PARTITION BY department
               ORDER BY wage DESC
           ) AS wage_rank
    FROM dbo.employees
)
SELECT *
FROM ranked
WHERE -- second rank
items.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        DENSE_RANK() OVER (
            PARTITION BY department
            ORDER BY wage DESC
        ) AS wage_rank
    FROM dbo.employees
)
SELECT *
FROM ranked
WHERE wage_rank = 2;
items.solutionExplanation: DENSE_RANK assigns the same rank to equal wages and does not leave gaps, so rank 2 means the second distinct wage level.
hints: Use DENSE_RANK for distinct wage levels.
items.pitfall: ROW_NUMBER gives unique row positions, not distinct wage levels, so ties can change which row is “second.”

items.title: Compare each weekday with previous occurrences
items.concept: PARTITION BY can separate Mondays from Tuesdays while ORDER BY sequences occurrences inside each weekday.
items.context: dbo.sensor_daily(date_value, weekday_number, visitors_count).
items.task: For each row, compute the average of the current and previous six occurrences of the same weekday.
items.starter:
SELECT *,
       AVG(visitors_count * 1.0) OVER (
           PARTITION BY weekday_number
           ORDER BY date_value
           ROWS BETWEEN --
       ) AS same_weekday_avg
FROM dbo.sensor_daily;
items.solution:
SELECT
    *,
    AVG(visitors_count * 1.0) OVER (
        PARTITION BY weekday_number
        ORDER BY date_value
        ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS same_weekday_avg
FROM dbo.sensor_daily;
items.solutionExplanation: Each weekday is isolated into its own time series, then the frame looks back across the previous six occurrences of that weekday.
items.pitfall: Without ORDER BY, “previous six” has no defined sequence.

items.title: Week-over-week percentage change
items.concept: LAG can supply the denominator for a change calculation on the current row.
items.context: dbo.sensor_daily(date_value, weekday_number, visitors_count).
items.task: Compute percentage change versus the previous occurrence of the same weekday.
items.starter:
WITH x AS (
    SELECT *,
           LAG(visitors_count) OVER (
               PARTITION BY weekday_number
               ORDER BY date_value
           ) AS previous_visitors
    FROM dbo.sensor_daily
)
SELECT *,
       -- percentage change
FROM x;
items.solution:
WITH x AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        LAG(visitors_count) OVER (
            PARTITION BY weekday_number
            ORDER BY date_value
        ) AS previous_visitors
    FROM dbo.sensor_daily
)
SELECT
    *,
    (visitors_count - previous_visitors) * 1.0
        / NULLIF(previous_visitors, 0) AS pct_change
FROM x;
items.solutionExplanation: The CTE exposes the prior value once. The outer query calculates (current - previous) / previous and protects against division by zero.
items.pitfall: The first row in each partition has no previous value, so pct_change is naturally NULL.

items.title: Number salaries inside each department
items.concept: ROW_NUMBER assigns a unique sequential position inside each partition according to the window ORDER BY.
items.context: dbo.employees(employee_name, department, wage).
items.task: Number employees from highest to lowest wage inside each department.
items.solution:
SELECT
    *,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY department
        ORDER BY wage DESC, employee_name
    ) AS wage_row_number
FROM dbo.employees;
items.solutionExplanation: The numbering restarts in each department. employee_name is added as a tie-breaker so tied wages still have stable ordering.
hints: Add a deterministic tie-breaker if possible.

items.title: Running average per sensor and weekday
items.concept: Windows can partition on multiple columns when the business series is defined by a composite key.

       AVG(visitors_count * 1.0) OVER (
           PARTITION BY -- two keys
           ORDER BY date_value
           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

FROM dbo.sensor_daily;

    *,
    AVG(visitors_count * 1.0) OVER (
        PARTITION BY sensor_id, weekday_number
        ORDER BY date_value
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_avg_visitors
FROM dbo.sensor_daily;

items.title: Rank sensors by their updated running average
items.concept: Complex analytics often layer window functions: one query computes a metric, then an outer query ranks that metric.
items.context: dbo.sensor_daily(sensor_id, weekday_number, date_value, visitors_count).
items.task: Compute running average per sensor + weekday, then DENSE_RANK sensors for each date by that running average descending.
items.solution:
WITH moving AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        AVG(visitors_count * 1.0) OVER (
            PARTITION BY sensor_id, weekday_number
            ORDER BY date_value
            ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
        ) AS running_avg_visitors
    FROM dbo.sensor_daily
)
SELECT
    *,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (
        PARTITION BY date_value
        ORDER BY running_avg_visitors DESC
    ) AS sensor_rank
FROM moving;
items.solutionExplanation: Window results cannot be nested directly inside another window function in the same SELECT. The CTE establishes the first window result, and the outer query performs the second window calculation.
hints: First window: sensor + weekday over time.
Second window: rank sensors within each date.
Use a CTE between the two stages.
items.pitfall: Trying to nest one window function directly inside another window function is not valid T-SQL.

items.concept: T-SQL commonly filters ranking results in an outer query because the window value is produced after WHERE.

items.task: Return exactly one top-paid employee per department using ROW_NUMBER and a CTE.

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY department
               ORDER BY wage DESC, employee_name
           ) AS rn
    FROM dbo.employees
)
SELECT *
FROM ranked
WHERE --

    SELECT
        *,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY department
            ORDER BY wage DESC, employee_name

    FROM dbo.employees
)
SELECT *
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

items.title: Understand ROWS vs RANGE with duplicate dates
items.concept: ROWS frames are based on physical row positions; RANGE frames can treat peer rows with equal ORDER BY values together.
items.context: dbo.sales_events(event_id, event_date, amount) may contain multiple rows for the same event_date.
items.task: Write a deterministic row-by-row running total using ROWS, even when event_date is duplicated.
items.solution:
SELECT
    *,
    SUM(amount) OVER (
        ORDER BY event_date, event_id
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_total
FROM dbo.sales_events;
items.solutionExplanation: ROWS advances one physical row at a time. Adding a unique event_id tie-breaker makes the ordering deterministic when multiple rows share a date.
hints: Add a unique ordering column such as event_id.
items.pitfall: Ordering only by a non-unique date leaves tied row ordering nondeterministic for row-by-row calculations.

materializedVariants.solution:
SELECT
    *,
    SUM(amount) OVER (
        ORDER BY event_date, event_id
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_total
FROM sales_events;
materializedVariants.explanation: ROWS advances one physical row at a time. Adding a unique event_id tie-breaker makes the ordering deterministic when multiple rows share a date. For this exercise the core SQL pattern is portable; schema prefixes are removed to keep the query close to the notebook/DuckDB style.

original.why: This pattern appears in data transformation, reconciliation, quality checks, reporting queries, and data-engineering interviews.
original.title: Understand ROWS vs RANGE with duplicate dates
original.concept: ROWS frames are based on physical row positions; RANGE frames can treat peer rows with equal ORDER BY values together.
original.context: dbo.sales_events(event_id, event_date, amount) may contain multiple rows for the same event_date.
original.task: Write a deterministic row-by-row running total using ROWS, even when event_date is duplicated.
original.solution:
SELECT
    *,
    SUM(amount) OVER (
        ORDER BY event_date, event_id
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_total
FROM dbo.sales_events;
original.solutionExplanation: ROWS advances one physical row at a time. Adding a unique event_id tie-breaker makes the ordering deterministic when multiple rows share a date.
hints: Add a unique ordering column such as event_id.
original.pitfall: Ordering only by a non-unique date leaves tied row ordering nondeterministic for row-by-row calculations.
