items.title: Create a high-value flag
items.concept: Conditional logic derives a new value without filtering rows.
items.context: orders has amount. Create is_high_value = 1 when amount >= 1000, otherwise 0.
items.task: Add the conditional column in the selected engine.
items.pitfall: A filter would remove low-value rows; the task is to keep them and label them.

tsql.starter:
SELECT *,
       CASE
           -- condition
       END AS is_high_value
FROM dbo.orders;
tsql.explanation: CASE returns one scalar value for each row.

duckdb.explanation: DuckDB uses standard CASE syntax.

bigquery.explanation: BigQuery supports both CASE and the compact IF(condition, true, false) function.

import numpy as np

df["is_high_value"] = np.where(
    # condition, true, false
)
pandas.solution:

df["is_high_value"] = np.where(df["amount"] >= 1000, 1, 0)
pandas.explanation: np.where vectorizes a simple two-way conditional.

df = df.withColumn(
    "is_high_value",
    F.when(# condition, 1).otherwise(0)
)

df = df.withColumn(
    "is_high_value",
    F.when(F.col("amount") >= 1000, 1).otherwise(0)

items.title: Revenue by customer
items.concept: Group rows by a business key and aggregate each group.
items.context: orders(customer_id, amount).
items.task: Return total amount per customer.
items.pitfall: Do not include row-level columns that are neither grouped nor aggregated.

tsql.starter:
SELECT customer_id,
       -- total
FROM dbo.orders
GROUP BY -- key
tsql.explanation: GROUP BY changes the grain to one row per customer.

duckdb.explanation: Standard aggregation syntax transfers directly.

bigquery.explanation: GoogleSQL uses the same core GROUP BY pattern.

result = (
    df.groupby(# key, as_index=False)
      .agg(# named aggregation)
)

      .agg(# aggregation)
)

result = (

items.title: Order count, revenue, and average by customer
items.concept: One grouping operation can compute several metrics at the same grain.
items.context: orders(customer_id, order_id, amount).
items.task: Return order_count, total_amount, and avg_amount per customer.
hints: All metrics use the same grouping key.
items.pitfall: Running three separate group operations creates needless work and makes joining results necessary.

tsql.starter:
SELECT customer_id,
       -- three aggregates
FROM dbo.orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
tsql.solution:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       SUM(amount) AS total_amount,
       AVG(amount) AS avg_amount
FROM dbo.orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
tsql.explanation: All aggregates are evaluated at the customer grain.

duckdb.explanation: DuckDB uses the same standard aggregate functions.

bigquery.explanation: The aggregation pattern is portable to BigQuery.

pandas.solution:
result = df.groupby("customer_id", as_index=False).agg(
    order_count=("order_id", "size"),
    total_amount=("amount", "sum"),
    avg_amount=("amount", "mean"),
)
pandas.explanation: pandas named aggregation maps output names to source-column/function pairs.

pyspark.starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
result = df.groupBy("customer_id").agg(
    # metrics
)
pyspark.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
result = df.groupBy("customer_id").agg(
    F.count("*").alias("order_count"),
    F.sum("amount").alias("total_amount"),
    F.avg("amount").alias("avg_amount"),
)
pyspark.explanation: PySpark accepts multiple aggregate expressions in a single agg call.

items.title: Join orders to customers
items.concept: An inner join keeps rows whose key exists on both sides.
items.context: orders(customer_id, order_id, amount); customers(customer_id, customer_name).
items.task: Attach customer_name to matching orders.
items.pitfall: Joining on the wrong key can multiply rows or silently mismatch records.

tsql.starter:
SELECT o.*, c.customer_name
FROM dbo.orders AS o
INNER JOIN dbo.customers AS c
    ON -- key
tsql.solution:
SELECT o.*, c.customer_name
FROM dbo.orders AS o
INNER JOIN dbo.customers AS c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
tsql.explanation: The ON predicate determines which row pairs match.

duckdb.starter:
SELECT o.*, c.customer_name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c
    ON -- key
duckdb.solution:
SELECT o.*, c.customer_name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
duckdb.explanation: JOIN without a modifier means INNER JOIN.

bigquery.starter:
SELECT o.*, c.customer_name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c
  ON -- key
bigquery.solution:
SELECT o.*, c.customer_name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
bigquery.explanation: GoogleSQL supports ON and USING join conditions.

pandas.explanation: DataFrame.merge is the database-style column join in pandas.

pyspark.starter:
result = orders.join(
    customers.select("customer_id", "customer_name"),
    # key and join type
)
pyspark.solution:
result = orders.join(
    customers.select("customer_id", "customer_name"),
    on="customer_id",
    how="inner",
)
pyspark.explanation: PySpark DataFrame.join can join directly by a shared key name.

items.title: Find orders with no customer match
items.concept: An anti join returns left-side rows that have no matching key on the right.
items.context: orders(customer_id,...); customers(customer_id,...).
items.task: Return orders whose customer_id is not present in customers.
hints: In SQL you can left join and test right-side NULL, or use NOT EXISTS.
items.pitfall: NOT IN can behave unexpectedly when the right side contains NULL.

tsql.starter:
SELECT o.*
FROM dbo.orders AS o
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM dbo.customers AS c
    WHERE -- key
);
tsql.solution:
SELECT o.*
FROM dbo.orders AS o
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM dbo.customers AS c
    WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id
);
tsql.explanation: NOT EXISTS expresses anti-join intent without NULL ambiguity.

duckdb.starter:
SELECT o.*
FROM orders o
ANTI JOIN customers c
    ON -- key
duckdb.solution:
SELECT o.*
FROM orders o
ANTI JOIN customers c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
duckdb.explanation: DuckDB supports an explicit ANTI JOIN form.

bigquery.explanation: NOT EXISTS is a clear portable anti-join pattern in GoogleSQL.

pandas.starter:
merged = orders.merge(
    customers[["customer_id"]],
    on="customer_id", how="left", indicator=True
)
result = merged[
    # left-only rows
]
pandas.solution:
merged = orders.merge(
    customers[["customer_id"]],
    on="customer_id", how="left", indicator=True
)
result = merged[merged["_merge"] == "left_only"].drop(columns="_merge")
pandas.explanation: The merge indicator reveals whether each row matched the right side.

    how=# anti join type
)

    on="customer_id",

items.concept: pandas merge can assert expected key cardinality to catch accidental row multiplication.
items.context: orders has many rows per customer_id; customers should have one row per customer_id.
items.task: Left-merge customers onto orders and validate many-to-one cardinality.
items.pitfall: A duplicated dimension key can silently multiply fact rows if you never validate the relationship.

pandas.starter:
result = orders.merge(
    customers,
    on="customer_id", how="left",
    validate=#
)
pandas.solution:
result = orders.merge(
    customers,
    on="customer_id", how="left",
    validate="many_to_one"
)
pandas.explanation: The validation raises if the right-side key is not unique as expected.

items.title: Calculate each row share of its customer total
items.concept: GroupBy.transform returns a same-length result aligned to the original rows.
items.context: orders(customer_id, amount).
items.task: Add customer_total and amount_share without collapsing the DataFrame.
items.pitfall: agg collapses to one row per group; transform is for group metrics returned to each original row.

pandas.explanation: transform broadcasts a group result back to rows at the original index.

pyspark.starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
w = Window.partitionBy("customer_id")
result = df.withColumn("customer_total", #).withColumn("amount_share", #)
pyspark.solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
w = Window.partitionBy("customer_id")
result = (df.withColumn("customer_total", F.sum("amount").over(w))
            .withColumn("amount_share", F.col("amount") / F.col("customer_total")))
pyspark.explanation: A partition-only Spark window is the closest equivalent to pandas transform for this case.

items.title: Recognize map and filter
items.concept: map transforms items; filter keeps items. In Python, comprehensions are often clearer, but both appear in codebases and interviews.
items.task: Use filter + lambda to keep positive row counts, then map them to thousands.
items.starter:
counts = [1200, 0, -1, 5200]
valid = filter(# predicate, counts)
thousands = list(map(# transform, valid))
items.solution:
counts = [1200, 0, -1, 5200]
valid = filter(lambda n: n > 0, counts)
thousands = list(map(lambda n: n / 1000, valid))
items.solutionExplanation: filter produces an iterator of positive values; map transforms those values; list materializes the final iterator.
items.pitfall: map and filter return iterators in Python 3, so inspect them by iterating or materializing them.

# Airflow 2 "Dataset" terminology became "Asset" in Airflow 3.

Dag authoring → airflow.sdk public interface
Dag parsing → independent dag-processor
Scheduling → scheduler
UI/API → api-server
Execution → executor/workers
Data dependency → Asset events

Airflow task run → RunEvent
inputs / outputs → Datasets
START / COMPLETE / FAIL → run lifecycle
Use lineage to scope downstream impact and backfills.
mentalModels: A DAG models dependencies, not the data itself.
Tasks should be retry-safe and ideally idempotent.
Pass small metadata through orchestration; store real datasets in data systems.
Airflow orchestrates work; it should not hide deterministic data errors behind repeated retries.
Queued and failed are different incident classes: a queued task may never have executed user code.
Backfills are production changes. Bound concurrency and validate each partition before widening the replay.
Airflow 3 DAG authors should target airflow.sdk, the documented public Task SDK interface.
Asset events model logical data dependencies; Airflow orchestrates metadata/events rather than moving the dataset itself.
Airflow 3 separates DAG processing and API serving more explicitly, so queued/parsing/UI incidents are different failure classes.
